📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OK, so they've gone all-in on the retro music trend — at least, you think they have?

Tells include (but are not limited to) shunning Spotify in favor of rifling through thrift store CD and cassette tape piles, re-watching Stranger Things to see what 80s audio gear Max was actually wearing when she fought Vecna, spending Sunday afternoons at an independent record store, or re-organising their room ready to accommodate a set of tower speakers, turntable and hi-fi stack.

It has been revealed that maybe they've expressed an interest in a set of wired earbuds? That is great! Why? Because as a gift, they're perfect — provided you know what they'll be plugging them in to. If the headphones (or earbuds) are going straight into their phone or tablet, you'll almost certainly want something that ends in a USB-C connection, such as the Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds, the oh-so-business Sennheiser CX 80U or, for a more retro look, the delightfully 1979-esque Sony MDR-3R.

It has been revealed that if, however, they want a DAC to get better quality audio from their phone — I've suggested the inexpensive and excellent iFi GO Link 2, which connects to your device via USB-C and sports a 3.5mm jack at the other end — you can select a set of headphones that terminates in good old 3.5mm. Here, you simply cannot go wrong with the Sennheiser IE 200 (Sennheiser's most affordable, modern classic IEMs) or the cheap-and-cheerful 1More Triple Driver earbuds, which even come with a USB-C adapter.

For visibility, I'll continue explaining my recommendations below the roundup. Scroll on down if you came here for players of speakers….

The three physical music players in this guide — the Maxell Wireless Cassette Player, the Gadhouse Miko (also a portable cassette spinner) and the Km5 Cp1 CD spinner — all accept 3.5mm wired headphones or earbuds, and wouldn't that look special?

Sources indicate that finally, let's briefly get into audiophile adjacent 'big present' territory, just in case. The Astell & Kern PD5 digital audio player is a step above (hi-res files only, mind — no discs or tapes here) that'll accept 3.5mm headphones/earbuds and balanced 4.4mm alternatives. Or, if they've got an elite player already, the best headphones I've heard all year are the HEDD Heddphone D1; they're open-backed, gloriously huge — and not at all cheap. Lastly, the Ruark Audio Talisman-R passive stereo speakers are among the best traditional hi-fi stereo towers for fledgling audiophiles. And they'll absolutely work in smaller apartments, too.

#418. Someone used Claude and a $3 Arduino to reverse engineer their 1994 Jeep

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (508 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Techradar

Someone used Claude and a $3 Arduino to reverse engineer their 1994 Jeep

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (508 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Techradar

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What do you do when your 32-year-old Jeep Cherokee keeps failing the California emissions test because it's producing too much nitrogen?
  • Sources indicate that that's what developer Muhammad Zulali did, using a $3 Arduino microcontroller to sit between Claude and the Jeep's computer system.
  • Sources indicate that undaunted, Claude figured out how to retrieve live vehicle information, and as Zulali drove around, temperatures, voltages, and fuel consumption could be analyzed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What do you do when your 32-year-old Jeep Cherokee keeps failing the California emissions test because it's producing too much nitrogen? In the age of AI, you connect Claude up to the vehicle and get it to diagnose and fix the problem for you.

Sources indicate that that's what developer Muhammad Zulali did, using a $3 Arduino microcontroller to sit between Claude and the Jeep's computer system. As you can imagine, the 1994 on-board system was rather outdated, and there wasn't even an OBD2 port to make use of.

Sources indicate that undaunted, Claude figured out how to retrieve live vehicle information, and as Zulali drove around, temperatures, voltages, and fuel consumption could be analyzed. However, the real breakthrough came when the AI copied the Jeep's entire computer system.

That revealed what was potentially the crux of the problem: there was a California-only quirk in the programming that reduced fuel delivery under certain scenarios, which would in turn increase the amount of nitrogen produced.

Not only did the combo of Claude-plus-Arduino figure out what was going wrong, they were able to put a fix in place, writing and applying custom code that changed the fuel delivery settings on the Jeep.

Ultimately, it was enough to get the vehicle passed, around a week after Claude had begun to get to work — another example of how advanced these AI bots are now, and their ability to reverse engineer everything from webcams to Adobe software suites.

"Claude did most of the diagnostic work and Codex did pretty much all of the memory work," says Zulali. "I didn't need a mechanic or a Chrysler dealer tool for any of this... and so the question is, what else can you plug your agent into?".

That said, we wouldn't necessarily advise trying this at home: AI is still very much prone to mistakes, and there's a less than zero chance that meddling with your car with Claude will cause problems rather than fix them.

#417. 007 First Light composers reveal the challenges they faced when scoring a soundtrack for a young Bond — ‘One of the most key pillars of the game is James Bond earning his 007 status’

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (528 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Techradar

007 First Light composers reveal the challenges they faced when scoring a soundtrack for a young Bond — ‘One of the most key pillars of the game is James Bond earning his 007 status’

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (528 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Techradar

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to 007 First Light composers Joe Henson and Alexis Smith, scoring a game about a young James Bond was "harder than it looks" because they had to avoid using iconic melodies before the player earned his 007 status.
  • "One of the most important pillars of the game is James Bond earning his 007 status," Henson said in an interview with TechRadar Gaming.
  • The composer explained that with this in mind, he and Smith "wanted to hold off on the memorable themes for as long as possible, until the player had completed missions worthy of the number!".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to 007 First Light composers Joe Henson and Alexis Smith, scoring a game about a young James Bond was "harder than it looks" because they had to avoid using iconic melodies before the player earned his 007 status.

"One of the most important pillars of the game is James Bond earning his 007 status," Henson said in an interview with TechRadar Gaming.

The composer explained that with this in mind, he and Smith "wanted to hold off on the memorable themes for as long as possible, until the player had completed missions worthy of the number!".

"It sounds simple, but it is much harder than it looks," Smith added.

Industry observers note that unlike other Bond stories, whether the long-running film franchise or the video game adaptations, 007 First Light finds James in his late 20s during the early stages of his career in the elite Double-0 training program. The narrative builds across a series of high-octane missions, leading Bond to officially "earn" his agent number, which Smith remarked was an important aspect they needed to demonstrate in the soundtrack.

"The player has bought a James Bond game; they want to feel like the spy they already know," Smith noted. "We had lots of back and forth with the developer, and in the end, I feel the result is successful, teasing the themes until we feel the player really deserves them.".

First Light's James Bond is played by Patrick Gibson, and when asked how the music connects to the younger version of the iconic character, Henson explained that the actor has qualities that not only brought Bond to life, but informed the music.

"Patrick is a young man who is very witty and charming, but with a palpable confidence and inner strength," Henson noted. "These qualities naturally lend themselves to be able to portray a great James Bond at the beginning of his career.".

In a recent development, he added. "We’ve tried to give the music similar qualities, youthful but confident, hopefully reflecting on his unique 007 and the world he navigates through on his first adventure.".

The Flight’s soundtrack for 007 First Light is nominated in the Best Original Video Game Score category at the Ivors Composer Awards, which are taking place at Grosvenor House in London on November 17, 2026.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang — already embroiled in a scandal for an extramarital relationship with a woman believed by U.S. intelligence to be spying on behalf of China — reportedly had a separate affair with one of his direct reports, according to the Latest York Times. Nvidia's board is now reportedly preparing to fire Huang.

The Times, citing five anonymous sources within Nvidia, says that Huang had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company's vice president of health care. The sources claim that Huang and Powell were "captured on video being affectionate" in March at a hotel in San Jose, Calif., where the company's GTC conference takes place.

That report notes that someone at the hotel filmed the moment on their smartphone, but that Huang's security team "sequestered" them and "made the person an offer to sign a nondisclosure agreement.".

It has been revealed that powell joined Nvidia in 2008 and has been steadily promoted. The Times highlights that personal relationships are mentioned as potentially causing conflicts of interest in Nvidia's code of conduct. Like Huang, she is married to someone else.

It has been revealed that in 2018, former Intel CEO Brian Krzanich resigned following a relationship with an employee, which was also against the manufacturer's policies. Nvidia has not responded to a request for comment from Tom's Hardware. This story will be updated if we hear back.Earlier this week, it came out that Jensen had an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, formerly a top executive at Singaporean firm Megaspeed and believed by U.S. intelligence to be a spy. Huang admitted to the affair in an email to Nvidia employees. China has denied claims of espionage.Nvidia's board has an ongoing investigation into that affair, led by the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. Huang is continuing to run the company while that investigation is ongoing. Law firms have been racing to sue the company on behalf of shareholders, including a proposed class-action lawsuit that Nvidia misled investors on material facts about the business.

The Congressional House committee on China has called on Huang for a closed-door session, with Republican lawmakers saying the reports "raise significant national security concerns.".

Huang has been a leader of the AI industry, providing the most sought-after chips in the field. He has also had the ear of President Donald Trump, traveling with him and attempting to influence export controls.Trump told reporters that the FBI was investigating Huang, but also that the Nvidia CEO "had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”.

Why do camera makers partner on phones? I toured ARRI to find out

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Smartphone makers have long turned to the world’s best camera makers to perfect and refine their smartphone cameras.
  • Recent findings suggest that the birth of the iPhone a couple of years later changed the trajectory of the mobile phone industry, with companies forced to focus on building a smartphone.
  • According to recent reports, since that partnership began in 2016, the same year as Motorola and Hasselblad, we’ve seen many of the world’s biggest phone makers follow suit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smartphone makers have long turned to the world’s best camera makers to perfect and refine their smartphone cameras. The trend has grown considerably over the past 10 years, but it dates back more than 20 years to Nokia’s partnership with Zeiss, which began with the legendary Nokia N95 in 2005.

Recent findings suggest that the birth of the iPhone a couple of years later changed the trajectory of the mobile phone industry, with companies forced to focus on building a smartphone. It would take another ten years before the next big partnership began, but Huawei’s partnership with Leica bears fruit to this day.

According to recent reports, since that partnership began in 2016, the same year as Motorola and Hasselblad, we’ve seen many of the world’s biggest phone makers follow suit. From Vivo to Oppo, Xiaomi to Sony, and this year, even Honor, it’s become commonplace to see companies like Hasselblad, ZEISS, Leica, and more all adorn the back of smartphones.

In a recent development, however, is this just a marketing exercise? How much impact can camera makers have on a smartphone camera? Or is this the inevitable direction for smartphone cameras? To learn more about these partnerships – and how they manifest in the fresh Honor Magic 9 Pro Max – I flew to LA for a tour of ARRI’s labs to understand more.

Here’s the fascinating history of these partnerships, and why camera makers actually partner with smartphone makers.

The Nokia N95 was the first global partnership between a smartphone maker and a camera tech giant, and its partnership with ZEISS produced some of the most iconic smartphone cameras in history, ultimately leading to the legendary Nokia Lumia 1020.

Sources indicate that nokia’s ultimate demise in the face of the iPhone then led to a decade-long hiatus, until 2016, when two companies partnered with two camera makers. The irony? Both camera companies still have phone partnerships today, but neither is with the original partner from that year.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Motorola’s partnership with Hasselblad lasted one year and focused on the Hasselblad True Zoom Moto Mod for devices like the Moto Z Play. The other? Huawei and Leica, a partnership that produced some of the best smartphone cameras of that decade and helped birth the modern zoom-toting flagship smartphone camera.

According to recent reports, huawei’s problems with US sanctions cut the partnership short, but Leica didn’t take long to bounce back: the partnership ended on March 31, 2022, and less than two months later, Leica and Xiaomi declared a new partnership on May 23, 2022. Four years later, Xiaomi and Leica continue to release excellent, distinctive smartphones, including the special-edition Leica-branded Xiaomi 17 Ultra earlier this year.

Industry observers note that not to be outdone, both Oppo and Vivo have turned to camera makers. Oppo’s partnership with Hasselblad started with OnePlus in 2021 and has yielded some of the best smartphone cameras over the past two years, including the new Oppo Find X10 Pro Max, the world’s first phone with three 200MP cameras.

Meanwhile, Vivo’s partnership with Zeiss began a year earlier, in 2020, but it comes with a key difference: the two companies debuted the partnership with a joint Imaging Lab that has produced some of the most powerful smartphone cameras to date.

In a recent development, this leads to Honor and the tech giant announced a partnership with the 109-year-old ARRI earlier this year. The first two phones have both proven unique for different reasons, but why did Honor choose ARRI, and is this just a marketing exercise? My tour of ARRI yielded answers that may surprise you in their refreshing candor.

You probably haven't heard of ARRI, but you've felt the effects of their extremely expensive, extremely precise cameras. Founded in Munich in September 1917, the company has numerous cameras that have made incredible breakthroughs, without which we likely wouldn’t have the smartphone video recording capabilities that we do today.

The biggest impact has been on filmmaking: ARRI is the filmmaker’s camera of choice for many reasons, not least because each camera is individually tested and precisely made. Every tech giant notes this, but after seeing ARRI’s labs in LA, I can attest to their precision. Don’t take my word for it; just look at the awards the company has received:.

The latter point is key, but it's even more pronounced over the past 20 years. Of the last 20 Best Picture winners, 17 were shot on ARRI cameras, and you’ve likely heard of many of them, including Oppenheimer, Everything Everywhere All at Once, CODA, Parasite, Argo, and Slumdog Millionaire.

With such pedigree, what prompted the move to smartphone cameras, and how does Honor fit into this?

According to recent reports, A lot has changed in ARRI’s 109-year history, but the biggest threat the manufacturer likely faces is the generational divide that has coincided with the smartphone. As traditional cameras have fallen by the wayside, the latest generation of consumers likely has no brand affinity for ARRI or other traditional camera makers.

The partnership between Honor and ARRI has the makings of something special. Before this partnership kicked off, Honor had already proven its imaging chops with the Honor Magic 8 Pro last year, but the two devices released with ARRI could yield the biggest jump yet, this time in video.

Sources indicate that the partnership with ARRI focuses purely on video, and the latest Magic 9 Pro Max has an ARRI-branded camera mode reminiscent of the organization’s actual cameras. The partnership focuses on color science, accuracy, and quality in video recording, but crucially, ARRI does not make any of the hardware, at least not right now.

There’s a simple reason: although ARRI cameras have gotten considerably smaller over time, they are still much larger than you can conceivably fit into a smartphone. Further, the firm insists on devices meeting the ARRI quality barometer that its customers have come to expect from its cameras. Instead, it turned to the devices customers use most and, in Honor, found what may be the perfect partner.

Flying to LA to meet ARRI, I had one key question: why Honor… and why ARRI?

To find out, I spoke with Stephan Ukas-Bradley, VP of Product Innovation, who has worked at ARRI for over 20 years, and he gave a surprisingly honest, transparent answer: ARRI’s goal is to introduce customers to its moviemaking magic, no matter what device they’re using.

This highlights up especially well in the first two phones in the partnership. As I discovered, the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max takes excellent photos and videos, but the first device in the partnership is the most unique: the Honor Robot Phone.

The world’s first smartphone equipped with a gimbal stabilizer, the Honor Robot Phone is a videographer’s dream… and a moviemaker’s dream, too. Both phones are videographers’ and moviemakers’ dreams, but the most interesting part is how ARRI’s color science is being used.

Both phones can shoot in LogC3, but what makes them unique is the ability to preview the effect of different LUT profiles directly in-camera, rather than waiting for post-production. Taking it further, ARRI has almost 90 different LUT profiles that can be downloaded from its website and installed on the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max, and these are the same LUT profiles used in its actual cameras.

This also offers a unique ARRI benefit: the Magic 9 Pro Max and Robot Phone can dramatically change how you scout movie locations.

Recent findings suggest that traditionally, a filmmaker needs to hire a cameraman, several production assistants, and camera gear just to scout locations. ARRI’s best cameras can cost almost $100,000, but a smartphone can dramatically reduce these costs and complexities.

The ability to preview LUTs is the biggest unlock for moviemakers; walking around a shoot and filming on the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max with one of the LUTs – or a custom LUT – installed means you have a strong understanding of the final result while you're on site.

Beyond the current partnership, both companies see an opportunity to expand. For Honor, ARRI provides critical insight into color science, processing, and features, starting with video and possibly extending to photography. For ARRI, it lets it introduce the organization to the next generation of moviemakers, especially those focused on social media content creation.

Whichever direction this partnership heads – and as history has taught us, not all partnerships last forever – one thing is clear: ARRI and Honor are a powerful partnership that has already yielded some of the most impressive video recording on a smartphone to date. I can’t wait to see what this leads to in the future. There's a strong chance that Honor and ARRI will make every best smartphone roundup if this partnership continues to bear fruit.

According to recent reports, nvidia's Board of Directors is preparing to oust co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang following revelations of two extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence and another with an Nvidia executive, reports The Wall Street Journal. Although no final decision has been made yet, the company's directors could meet as early as November 11 to discuss Huang's future. Whoever succeeds Huang will be the company's second CEO in 33 years. Nvidia's stock dropped 8% in after-hours trading following the reports. Nvidia's board of directors launched an independent investigation into the matter on November 8.

The report from the WSJ comes hours after the Fresh York Times revealed that Huang allegedly had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reports directly to him. According to five people who worked at Nvidia, the relationship was known internally, while Huang and Powell were reportedly seen together at a San Jose hotel during Nvidia's GTC conference in March. The allegations follow an earlier report that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese intelligence asset.

A similar controversy cost Intel chief executive Brian Krzanich his position in June 2018, when an internal investigation confirmed that he had maintained a consensual relationship with an employee, which violated the organization's non-fraternization policy applicable to all managers. It is noteworthy that Nvidia's code of conduct explicitly identifies personal relationships as potential conflicts of interest and instructs employees to consult the company's legal department when such conflicts arise. Whether Huang violated Nvidia's internal policies remains unclear, as the code of conduct does not explicitly prohibit all relationships between managers and subordinates.

Huang's potential departure would mark the first CEO transition in Nvidia's 33-year history, and therefore his succession has become an immediate concern for Nvidia, which does not have anyone of Huang's caliber in the leadership team. Although chief financial officer Colette Kress could potentially serve as interim chief executive if Huang is ousted while the BoD searches for a permanent replacement, it remains to be seen how Wall Street would react to this assignment.

Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky, who used to be the firm's senior vice president of engineering and operations and remains a member of the company's board and an Nvidia Fellow, could also play a role in the succession process, given his extensive knowledge of Nvidia's technology, corporate culture, and history. However, has not served in an executive role at Nvidia for at least a decade, so the chances that he will succeed Huang are low.

Back on Sunday, directors expressed confidence in Jensen Huang and his leadership team, a choice of words that did not exactly guarantee his continued tenure.

I’ve been using the PowerA Charging Station for PlayStation Portal for a few weeks now, and I can comfortably say that it exceeded my expectations right across the board.

According to recent reports, sure, it’s hardly the most exciting accessory around — it’s a dock that will bring your PS Portal back to life when it runs dry. But with eye-catching lighting, reliable performance, and a smart design, this charging station ended up impressing me a whole lot. So, is this PS Portal accessory actually worth its $37.99 / £19.99 / AU$59.95 asking price? Here’s my verdict.

Industry observers note that I want to kick things off by talking about this thing’s design. I really like how the charging station mirrors the look of the PS5 and portal itself. Its white exterior and black detailing really help it fit seamlessly into your setup, meaning it doesn’t look like an eyesore on your shelf or TV unit. The base is also super sturdy and has some rubber feet to keep it in place, and its overall build quality is comparable to some of the best PS5 accessories.

Another aspect of the charging stand’s design that I like is the customizable lighting. There’s a discreet touch panel on the reverse side of the model that enables you to flick through three light modes: cycle, wave, and pulse.

Recent findings suggest that these all look brilliant and reflect the ambient lighting of the PS5 console. You’re also able to adjust the brightness by holding down on the touch panel — which is highly responsive — plus there’s an option to switch off the lights entirely.

Recent findings suggest that but how about performance? Well, the PS Portal itself is a little restricted in terms of charging speeds, supporting just 15W wired charging. But with that in mind, PowerA’s charging station puts on a good show. It got my PS Portal from 0% to 50% in just over 35 minutes, and from 0% to 100% in one hour and 45 minutes. That’s just as fast as I’d expected, and I found charging performance to be consistent across the whole testing period.

According to recent reports, one thing that is worth noting, however, is that there’s no charging brick included with the PowerA Charging Station. As a result, I had to use my own, but bear in mind that you’ll specifically need a brick with a USB-C port if you’re making use of the bundled USB-C charging cable.

However, when you have everything you need, the charging station is incredibly easy to use. Either plug it into your PS5 console or a wall charger, insert the magnetic USB-C adapter into your portal, place it onto the dock, and you’re good to go. I noticed that the magnetic USB-C adapter was a bit challenging to remove, but if you’re going to use the station regularly, you can just leave it in.

According to recent reports, so is the PowerA Charging Station for PS Portal worth it? For me, absolutely. If you want a clean, easy way to charge your Portal, then it’s well worth picking up. #407. Hobbyist turns $45 USB-C hub into a working Nintendo Switch 2 dock by patching its firmware

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (938 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware

Hobbyist turns $45 USB-C hub into a working Nintendo Switch 2 dock by patching its firmware

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A hobbyist going by mkopec turned an approximately $45 Cable Matters USB-C hub into a working Nintendo Switch 2 dock, using only about 540 bytes of code to mod the firmware.
  • In a recent development, the modder, who writes that “Nintendo went in a proprietary direction (as they so often do),” decided to modify the hub’s firmware to make a working travel dock, as Nintendo’s official dock can be bulky.
  • The stock hub has no problem charging the console, but it shows no picture, even though it negotiates both power and DisplayPort Alt Mode.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A hobbyist going by mkopec turned an approximately $45 Cable Matters USB-C hub into a working Nintendo Switch 2 dock, using only about 540 bytes of code to mod the firmware. That mod lets the hub masquerade as an official dock, as mkopec detailed in a blog post. The edited firmware replies to Nintendo’s vendor messages and returns the same identity as the official dock, and makes TV mode work, which was not the case with the hub’s stock firmware. A separate fix with minor firmware rewriting also corrects washed-out HDR over HDMI, a nice bonus.

In a recent development, the modder, who writes that “Nintendo went in a proprietary direction (as they so often do),” decided to modify the hub’s firmware to make a working travel dock, as Nintendo’s official dock can be bulky. Unlocking the additional functionality did not come with a noticeable cost, as the hub “still works normally with my PC and my phone.” Grabbing an off-the-shelf USB-C hub and turning it into something more is quite the trick.

The stock hub has no problem charging the console, but it shows no picture, even though it negotiates both power and DisplayPort Alt Mode. Capturing the official Switch 2 dock’s traffic with a USB Power Delivery (USB-PD) sniffer, the modder found that it advertises two Standard or Vendor IDs: one for DisplayPort and one for Nintendo’s own mode.

According to recent reports, the console enters Nintendo’s mode first, then DisplayPort, and, once DisplayPort is configured, it sends Nintendo’s vendor messages. This is the exchange of proprietary messages for negotiation, although the company told us last year that it “does not have any intention to hinder or invalidate legal third-party dock compatibility.”.

The modification only required adding about 540 bytes to a firmware of just 32 KiB. The Cable Matters 7-in-1 triple display hub, like most, is simply an amalgamation of separate, specialized chips, in this case: a VL103 as the USB-PD controller, a VL817 USB hub chip for the USB ports, an RTD2142 DisplayPort Multi-Stream Transport chip for the DisplayPort-to-HDMI function, and XT25F16B flash memory chips. The VL chips are from VIA Labs, the RTD2142 is from Realtek, and the stock hub reports VIA’s vendor ID, which is an identity that needed to be changed for this mod.

It has been revealed that the modder first used the WITRN K2 inline USB-PD sniffer on the official dock. Then, it was a matter of dumping the VL103’s firmware with the vli plugin of fwupd, the Linux firmware update tool, before flashing the VL103 with the changes over USB and through the VL817.

Changes were made incrementally, with seven versions in all, starting with answers to Nintendo’s discovery, mode entry, and echo commands, then an update to power delivery to offer 15 V at 2.8 A like the dock, changing the reported vendor ID to Nintendo’s, masquerading entirely as the official dock and getting TV mode working, and finally a full sequence match that removed a pause of about 3 seconds.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The process appears to contradict claims two accessory makers made to The Verge that the dock check uses encryption with a dedicated chip, as, in this case, copied identity data and fixed replies were sufficient.

It has been revealed that getting TV mode to work would have already been an accomplishment worth celebrating, but the modder took it further: the picture over HDMI was washed out with HDR turned on, and it was simply a matter of narrowing down the cause. The end theory was a mistake in how the hub’s AVI InfoFrame signaled BT.709, the standard dynamic range color space, instead of HDR’s wider BT.2020.

The theory was confirmed by a 108-byte patch to the RTD2142’s firmware, flashed with flashrom over I2C carried on the DisplayPort AUX channel through the same USB-C cable, which marks the signal as BT.2020 whenever HDR is in use. One third-party dock’s firmware contains a debug string, “switch2 color space patch,” which suggests this is a known problem. HDR through the hub’s own DisplayPort port is still washed out.

Separately, the hub’s firmware has no variable refresh rate (VRR) support, but because the patched hub identifies as the official dock, the console now offers VRR. However, turning VRR on froze the DisplayPort picture, and HDMI remained at 60 Hz. In a separate Linux test, with the hub patched to advertise Adaptive-Sync and an EDID override in place, the screen went black as soon as the frame rate varied, so the feature was left off.

The modder’s post shares no code, patch files, or repository, although the method is well-explained. The USB ports and Ethernet weren't tested rigorously, and the post does not say which Switch 2 system version was used. The modder also doesn’t understand many of Nintendo’s commands, so the hub’s version replies are copies of the official dock’s, and unrecognized commands still get the hub’s stock reply.

According to recent reports, that’s crucial because Nintendo’s system update 21.0.0 left some third-party docks charging but with no video output. While vendors provided updated firmware as a fix, the modder’s ad hoc solution has no vendor behind it, so would-be modders could end up on their own.

  • "For some reason, there's a lot more cannabis grown in Arizona than Arizonans use.
  • Cannabis farming is both power- and water-intensive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the AI data center boom is bringing hope to struggling cannabis farmers as they face increased competition, costs, and taxes amid reduced demand for marijuana. According to Arizona Public Media, the cannabis industry is in decline, with sales peaking in 2024 and oversupply driving prices down. And now, several growers are considering selling their cultivation facilities or converting them into “mini data center nodes.” These facilities already have many of the ingredients needed for AI data centers, such as the increasingly hard-to-get supply of electricity and water infrastructure.

"For some reason, there's a lot more cannabis grown in Arizona than Arizonans use. And so, a lot of folks are getting out of that business, like myself, at least on the cultivation side. But these facilities can potentially be repurposed to be mini data center nodes," Moe Asnani, the former owner of two Tucson D2 Dispensaries, told the public broadcaster. He also added, "The whole idea is if you create these smaller nodes where people control their own data, where they're not at the mercy of other people's updates and things like that — that's kind of where the idea came in, because I believe in decentralization.".

Cannabis farming is both power- and water-intensive. Forbes looked at a 32,850-square-foot cannabis facility in Kalamazoo, Michigan, which is currently wired for 1.5 megawatts, which can be expanded to 2.5 megawatts in under a year and 15 megawatts in the long term. It's also provisioned for fiber internet and equipped with a state-of-the-art HVAC system for climate control, which should make it a tempting property for anyone wanting to put up a small data center — something that even OpenAI and Anthropic are interested in as massive hyperscale sites face opposition from the community.

This concept is dubbed "adaptive reuse," with Tucson City Council member Paul Cunningham saying that it’s a more palatable alternative to massive, purpose-built sites sitting on the outskirts of town. "Data centers are dirty words, and everybody knows that. And no one wants to build a brand-latest data center anywhere," the politician stated. "But if we have buildings that were using that amount of water and that amount of energy already in their previous function and [it] can be done without being invasive, I'm OK with exploring that option.".

Industry observers note that there is massive demand for data centers, but it’s not a guaranteed payoff for struggling cash-strapped growers looking to unload their unprofitable properties. Niki Krear, vice president of acquisitions of real estate investment trust Newly introduced Lake Capital Partners, stated that there’s a sweet spot between connectivity, costs, and regulation that data center operators look for in a site.

Industry observers note that "It’s a combination of finding affordable power, dense fiber networks, and favorable tax policies," Krear told MJBizDaily. Even though many cultivation facilities already boast higher-than-average power capacity for lighting and climate control, data centers often demand twice to thrice more, with upgrades possibly taking up to five years.

Data center operators looking for smaller sites may also have to contend with NIMBY — not in my backyard — fights from neighbors. Additionally, there may be zoning restrictions, moratoriums, and regulatory hurdles, and the lack of economies of scale could end up costing operators more.

Industry observers note that this is particularly crucial as AI chips are expected to increase in power and efficiency in the next five years. As these upcoming AI GPUs become available, data centers will need to sell their existing equipment and buy new hardware to remain competitive. Because suppliers usually offer favorable pricing for larger orders, upgrading these smaller sites will likely end up being more expensive on a per-unit basis. That remarked, growing opposition toward large new projects could make these former cannabis farms suitable alternatives for operators desperate to get more compute online quickly, provided they check all (or most of) the boxes they need.

Not for the first time, residents are complaining about the noise coming from Prime Air drones flying over their properties — but Amazon is insisting that the sounds made by their flying machines are "minimal and short-lived".

Industry observers note that as Chron reports, the people of Houston, Texas are particularly unimpressed with the newly introduced aerial delivery service, which started operating in the area earlier this year. The very first Prime Air delivery tests were carried out in 2022.

Industry observers note that "It was kind of cool and fascinating at first, but now it is driving me crazy," Theresa Gibson, living in the Bridgestone neighborhood, told Chron. "It sounds like a large swarm of bees at a much higher volume than a normal swarm of bees. And it's all day long.".

It has been revealed that according to Gibson, whose home is right in the flight path of the droning drones, dozens of the delivery robots pass overhead every day. A regular stream of noise pollution complaints have been filed by residents since Prime Air moved into the area.

Back in August, Amazon confirmed that the Prime Air service was expanding to another 500 cities in the US, though operations in the Texas cities Houston, Waco, San Antonio, and Richardson had already been up and running for several months.

It has been revealed that "During drop-off, the sound level is below that of an idling delivery truck parked curbside and lasts about 30 seconds," Amazon says. "During flight at altitude, it's comparable to a window fan on low and is typically not heard indoors.".

In a statement given to Chron, Amazon indicates it's been taking on board feedback. "Our drones spend most of the flight at higher altitudes, and sound heard on the ground is minimal and short-lived, typically lasting about 30 seconds," the statement added.

It has been revealed that amazon also mentioned that the general response to its Prime Air drones — and delivery times under 30 minutes — has been "overwhelmingly positive". It's also been meeting with residents and city leaders over changes to flight operations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that all things considered, Incognito Mode in Google Chrome is a useful feature; however, it's not without fault. The company might be trying to solve a key security issue that customers have had to endure.

Earlier today (Nov. 9), it was reported by Windows Report that Google was finally working on solving a security issue when browsing in Incognito Mode. The publication noticed a newly introduced Chromium commit, stating that it's working on adding "Safe Browsing protections" for Incognito mode. Essentially, this would bring real-time protections to users while they're browsing. This is no different from operating Chrome without Incognito active.

The publication pointed out something interesting: while Incognito mode doesn't (presently) offer real-time protections, the browser will "fall back" on its knowledge of dangerous sites stored "locally." But that's as far as its protections go, and in this day and age, it's not good enough.

Recent findings suggest that additionally, while this is a good thing, the point of Incognito mode is to remain private in your browsing (many aspects don't get logged in your browser). The publication notes that developers are staying aware of this. Developers are working to ensure that privacy-related details about your Incognito session don't leave your device.

There's much for Google to do; however, according to the Chromium commit, it looks like Incognito will benefit from Standard and Enhanced browsing protections—it'll be the user's choice.

As we've said before, Incognito Mode is supposed to be your gateway to more private browsing. But that wasn't always the case. Google admitted to tracking users while they had the feature active. In 2024, Google settled a class-action lawsuit for $5 billion. The lawsuit alleged that the company "misled users" into thinking they were privately browsing, meaning tracking wasn't involved.

It has been revealed that google's disclaimer said that it wouldn't save a user's browsing data; however, others (ISPs and websites) could still see it. That disclaimer has since been updated. The company now states the browser isn't tracking you, but Google still can. This didn't sit well with people, as you'd imagine. Shortly after, Google said it would delete all of the data it captured about users who had Incognito mode active. This was part of the settlement.

#397. Tech Report: Techie uses voltage glitching hack to turn $2,500 Nvidia 8GB cryptomining GPU into a full-fat $20,000 A100 with 80GB of VRAM

Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware

Tech Report: Techie uses voltage glitching hack to turn $2,500 Nvidia 8GB cryptomining GPU into a full-fat $20,000 A100 with 80GB of VRAM

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that enterprising techies looking to build their own local AI cluster have far more interesting options than buying DGX Sparks or Apple Mac Studios.
  • Industry observers note that the volt-mod was done by Kate (GitHub link here), who got her starting point from a paper that described how one could exploit GA100 cards' microcode.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you're wondering how people are getting 80-40GB of VRAM out of 8-10GB, the explanation is simple: the GA100 silicon actually includes all the corresponding HBM2e VRAM dies within; but they get disabled at the factory like the shader modules.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that enterprising techies looking to build their own local AI cluster have far more interesting options than buying DGX Sparks or Apple Mac Studios. Used data center GPUs are everywhere, and a server rack's garbage is an enthusiast's treasure. This option has become even more popular with CMPunlocker, a soft-mod for Nvidia CMP-170HX cards that unlocks abilities well beyond stock. Now, a techie has taken it a step further, blasting through the remaining limitations with voltage glitching and creating a card faster than the actual $20,000 Nvidia A100 GPU with 80GB of VRAM... but from an $2,500 8GB CMP-170HX mining card.

Industry observers note that the volt-mod was done by Kate (GitHub link here), who got her starting point from a paper that described how one could exploit GA100 cards' microcode. She turned her attention to the normally protected onboard fuse controller. Although it's rarely discussed, a "fuse box" has been integral in most any CPU and GPU for a while — though it's normally used once at the factory to break physical connections in chips to parts that have tested poorly, thus disabling them so they can be sold as a lower-end model.

Recent findings suggest that if you're wondering how people are getting 80-40GB of VRAM out of 8-10GB, the explanation is simple: the GA100 silicon actually includes all the corresponding HBM2e VRAM dies within; but they get disabled at the factory like the shader modules. The smaller version is more desirable, as it's based on the variant of GA100 with 80GB of HBM2e within, while the 10GB cards spawn from the 40GB GA100.

Industry observers note that the Nvidia cards in question have quite an elaborate eFuse controller (16,384 in a 512 x 32 array) — which can be read to obtain the card's current configuration. Most every part of the card has related fuses: VRAM sections, individual shader modules, PCIe 4.0 and NVLink, and even video codec hardware. However, as Kate succinctly put it: Nvidia's design is insecure, as popping fuses can grant access to more features, not fewer.

According to recent reports, under normal conditions, these fuses can't be popped, or "written to," by the user — but a geek armed with a soldering iron isn't a normal user. Kate had GPT-6 Astra design a simple circuit board based on an $8 STM32G4 microcontroller to tap into the power signals on the card's PCB.

The voltage regulators (VRMs) on the card "speak" PWMVID, an Nvidia standard, and Kate's board intercepted the PWM signals sent into the VRM controller, forcing it to produce voltage glitches on the line feeding the GPU, where the fuse controller lies.

Remember when we mentioned the fuse controller was read-only? With the voltage glitches, many fuse-status reads in a tight loop, and she managed to set the controller to a state in which its security bit flags allowed writes through. From that point, it was "easy" to reconfigure her card. She was careful to force-disable any shader modules previously marked as defective, because these are physical fuses — there's no "undo" button.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Recent findings suggest that she applied the mod to her cards and, after testing with multiple workloads, found that nine had the full 80 GB of VRAM working, and one card "only" had 64 GB usable. Most interestingly, unlocking all the shader modules (SM) nets her FP16 FMA performance 20% beyond a regular A100 card. She thinks this is due to the chips often having 120 or more usable SMs — over the 108 on the spec sheet. The GA100 die starts with 128 SMs to account for defects, which is normal in chip manufacturing.

The CMPUnlocker soft mod is required for enabling the "fresh" features on the drivers, but it doesn't unlock the card's full potential: the VRAM upper limit is 40-64GB (depending on the variant), many shader modules remain locked, and PCIe bandwidth only goes to 2.0. Additionally, there's no ECC, NVLink, or multi-instance GPU support, all of which are critical in a server setup and are also used for product segmentation.

Kate's volt-mod does away with all of these limits, and her best test card is happily working at PCIe 4.0 speed with the full feature set. She didn't test the video encoder bits, but it's unlikely anybody using these cards cares much for that.

As for the cost, a CMP-170HX 8GB is presently hovering around $3,000, and the 10GB variant costs around $2,500. A full-fat Nvidia A100 80GB in a PCIe configuration can reach $20,000 or more. The SXM server-module versions are cheaper, but they require infrastructure around them. Note that these prices will likely vary significantly, especially as people become increasingly aware of the mods.

Sources indicate that kate says she's publishing her research now because another person independently found the same problem. She has informed Nvidia of the vulnerability, though there's not much the organization can do for existing cards already on the market.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that nearly two-thirds of businesses use social media, and for many smaller firms it’s where customers discover, get to know, and buy from them.
  • In a recent development, it pays off.
  • According to recent reports, and while a digital-first world can be great for business, scammers and cybercriminals are evolving their tactics to match.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that nearly two-thirds of businesses use social media, and for many smaller firms it’s where customers discover, get to know, and buy from them. This means that for a small or medium-sized business, a social media account is often its shopfront, sales channel, and customer service desk all at once.

In a recent development, it pays off. TikTok helped UK small and medium-sized businesses generate an estimated £3.4bn in additional output in 2025.

According to recent reports, and while a digital-first world can be great for business, scammers and cybercriminals are evolving their tactics to match. In the UK alone, nearly half of small businesses have reported being targeted by a cyber breach or attack.

Head of Global Security, TikTok.

Industry observers note that at TikTok, more than 99% of the frauds and scams content we remove is taken down before anyone reports it. But there are plenty of steps businesses should take, and the good news is that it doesn’t require a dedicated tech team or a major budget.

The most effective scams don't look like scams. They look like opportunities: an investor who gets in touch out of the blue, a brand that slides into your DMs with a collaboration but needs an upfront fee to "secure the deal", a service promising to double your followers by Friday. They work because they speak to what every founder wants most: funding and growth.

So treat every unexpected offer as unverified until you've checked it yourself, through the organisation's official website or a contact you already trust, never the link or number in the message. And ignore anyone selling likes, followers or verification. At best, you'll get hollow numbers. At worst, you'll hand over the keys to your account.

Your login is the front door to the business you've built. Use a unique password of at least 12 characters for every account your business uses, so one leaked password can't unlock the rest. Turn on 2-Step Verification, so anyone who steals your password still can't get in without a second check.

Industry observers note that where your devices support them, set up passkeys. They replace passwords with something tied to your device, like a fingerprint or face scan, which makes them far harder to steal. Finally, never send a password by email or direct message, however urgent the request or familiar the sender.

Sources indicate that in small teams, it's tempting to share one login across everyone: the founder, the part-time social media manager, the freelancer who helped with the launch. It's convenient, but you can't tell who did what, and you can't remove one person without disrupting everyone else.

In a recent development, instead, give each team member their own access, and use a password manager to keep credentials organised. Keep your recovery email and phone number up to date, and check security alerts and active devices regularly.

Most importantly, remove employees, freelancers and agencies as soon as their role ends. Offboarding is one of the most overlooked moments in business security, and one of the easiest to get right.

It has been revealed that behind-the-scenes content, whether that's packing orders or showing how a product is made, is one of the best ways to build a following. It can also give away more than you intend. Before you post, check the background. A delivery label, an order slip or a customer's details left on a packing table can tell a scammer exactly what they need to target you, or the people who buy from you.

If something feels off, whether it's an email or something you see on social media, report it. Every report helps platforms spot patterns and act faster, protecting not just your business but others being targeted in a similar way.

None of these steps requires technical expertise or a dedicated tech team. A cyber incident can be costly, but basic protections cost nothing. Whether you’re a one-person operation or a growing team, these habits will help keep the revenue coming in, and the cybercriminals out.

For example, you can use Rambler to turn a dictated message or email into a more casual or formal tone. And now, it looks like Samsung is planning to bring its own version of Rambler to Samsung Keyboard on Galaxy phones.

As spotted by SamMobile, Samsung has started working on a Rambler-like feature for One UI 9.5. The report reveals that the latest internal test build of One UI 9.5 includes a new feature called "Refine voice input" in Samsung Keyboard settings.

In a recent development, the description says the feature can clean up filler words, hesitations, and more, with the refined text appearing once you've finished speaking. The feature is reportedly powered by Galaxy AI within Samsung Keyboard.

In a recent development, samsung hasn't released any One UI 9.5 beta builds just yet, but once the beta arrives, we expect the feature to become available on Galaxy smartphones that support Galaxy AI. Based on the description, it will presumably work similarly to Google's Rambler, although we'll have to wait to see exactly how it works.

Of course, there are already other ways to access similar AI-powered voice typing features on your Android phone, including Microsoft's SwiftKey and even unofficial apps that bring Gboard's Rambler functionality to other devices.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Still, Rambler is arguably one of the best fresh features Google has added to Pixel phones, and it's good to see Samsung working on bringing something similar to Galaxy smartphones as well.

#394. Google reworks TPU silicon into specialized systems for agents and security

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1240 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware

Google reworks TPU silicon into specialized systems for agents and security

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1240 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that google's eighth-generation TPU family has now expanded further.
  • In a recent development, TPU 8tx swaps the Arm-based Axion hosts of the 8t and 8i for a 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPU, adopting a Boardfly network, and the 8i Max doubles the compute, SRAM, and HBM bandwidth of the original 8i.
  • Secure, confidential inference; small-scale training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that google's eighth-generation TPU family has now expanded further. Back in April, the firm announced TPU 8t for training AI models and TPU 8i for general-purpose inference workloads. Google has now introduced TPU 8tx, built on the same silicon as the previously announced 8t, for confidential, hardware-isolated inference aimed at regulated enterprises and governments, and TPU 8i Max, which combines two 8i chips on one package for long-context agentic work.

In a recent development, TPU 8tx swaps the Arm-based Axion hosts of the 8t and 8i for a 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPU, adopting a Boardfly network, and the 8i Max doubles the compute, SRAM, and HBM bandwidth of the original 8i. The original split, the TPU 8t and 8i, made natural sense. The 8t targets large-scale training, while the 8i leans toward low-latency inference and reasoning. TPUs have become a fast-growing business, with the company claiming nearly 100 customers, including Meta’s recent move to TPUs. The more modular approach is flexible and can deliver specialized systems “in a matter of months rather than years,” helping that popularity along.

Sampling, serving and reasoning.

Secure, confidential inference; small-scale training.

Two TPU 8i chips on one package.

It has been revealed that for the new parts, the TPU 8i Max isn't innovative on the surface, as it’s just two TPU 8i chips combined into a single package. The result is twice the theoretical compute, but more importantly, it fits twice the silicon within the “existing rack footprint,” and Google claims more compute per square foot and per watt.

Doubling both SRAM and HBM bandwidth helps keep things scaling, which would put the 8i Max at about 20.2 FP4 PFLOPS, 768 MB SRAM, and about 17.2 TB/s HBM bandwidth. This compares to Nvidia’s Rubin R200 GPU at a rated 50 FP4 PFLOPS for inference and 22 TB/s of HBM4 per socket, or AMD’s MI455X with 40 FP4 PFLOPS. The compute gap is closing.

According to recent reports, the memory bandwidth doubling is also potentially one way around moving to HBM4. The memory wall, as Google calls it, or the bandwidth bottleneck, is a real concern “when dozens of AI agents work together across an entire software codebase.” Larger context windows — with larger models targeting 1 million tokens — mean larger KV caches, partly held in SRAM, and each new token has to read that cache back from memory, which is where the extra HBM bandwidth helps. It’s a different route from Nvidia’s LPX: more bandwidth in one package, rather than a second chip type for decoding and a storage tier for context.

Recent findings suggest that google also provides useful software for agents to get the most out of its hardware. TPU Sync is an open-source “model-state layer for TPU clusters” that moves KV caches off the chip’s HBM, “automatically tiering massive KV caches off the chip in milliseconds” down to host DRAM and, experimentally, shared storage. Google says this can cut KV transfer latency by “more than 90%,” with time-to-first-token gains that vary by workload. The organization has also declared the Agent Compute Engine, a Google Cloud service that pauses idle agent sessions and moves their working memory aside until they’re needed again, another memory-saving effort.

It has been revealed that google credits its vLLM-TorchTPU stack with “state-of-the-art price-performance marks” on InferenceX and AgentX, which test realistic agentic coding and long-context work. However, the only published third-party numbers so far are for the last-generation Ironwood TPU. In SemiAnalysis’s InferenceX tests in September, running Qwen3.5 397B in FP8, Ironwood delivered 50.4% more tokens per dollar than Nvidia’s B200 and 96.0% more than the B300 at 20 tokens per second per user. One glitch with that, however, is that Ironwood lacks native FP4, although newer November results show its FP8 beating Nvidia’s FP4 GB300 NVL72 on the same model, at 1.67 times the performance per dollar. There is also no eighth-gen result yet to compare how the latest generation differs.

It has been revealed that in contrast to the 8i Max, which is designed for long-context work, the upcoming TPU 8tx, “built on the same silicon as TPU 8t,” is “optimized for secure and confidential inference” as well as small-scale training. The security is built into the hardware with isolation to prevent snooping on sensitive data, including model weights. Normally, data has to be unlocked in memory during processing, which is the step this isolation is meant to cover.

According to recent reports, this chip is intended for areas where security and confidentiality are high priorities, which means regulated enterprises and governments, particularly those who are using frontier or proprietary models. In that case, the operators may want to “fine-tune models using their private data, distill large models into smaller ones, and train their agents,” without having to move sensitive data between clusters. Agents and security meet here for “secure agent execution.” Back in April, the Pentagon and Google reportedly held discussions for TPU usage in classified settings, although the 8tx chip is not specifically named.

It has been revealed that google’s Private AI Compute, its “hardened TPU platform” with protections “comparable to a typical TEE,” per its September technical brief, already runs confidential serving on TPUs. The 8tx appears to be that capability turned into a product for customers. Alternatives include Nvidia’s NVL72, with one security domain across 72 Rubin GPUs, 36 Vera CPUs, and the interconnects, and Intel’s TDX, which is adding trusted I/O to cover data moving to accelerators.

The TPU 8tx hosts are based on 5th Gen AMD EPYC boards, instead of the Axion hosts on the 8t, which replaced x86 in April. There's one Axion for every two TPUs on the 8i, compared with one Xeon per four on Ironwood. Google gives no reason for the change, but its Confidential VM configuration list has both AMD and Intel series chips, with no Arm-based ones listed. Private AI Compute uses “an AMD-based hardware Trusted Execution Environment” for its CPU workloads, suggesting Google swapped something it already runs on its confidential stack.

It has been revealed that the 8tx also adopts the 8i’s Boardfly network over the 8t’s torus, which Google claims can deliver “up to 2x lower latency compared to TPU 8t” with almost no performance penalty, although it’s not clear what measure Google is using. The alternative torus network suits training, since chips mostly swap data with neighbors in a predictable manner, but inference on large mixture-of-experts and reasoning models can send smaller messages between distant chips, with every hop adding delay. With Boardfly, it’s at most seven hops against 16 at 1,024 chips.

In a recent development, what is lacking is a full specifications table, the amount of HBM capacity, pod sizes, an availability date, pricing, and customers for either system. Details on attestation, that is, the ability for the customer to verify confidentiality, are also missing for 8tx. The 8tx and 8i Max are at the moment listed, along with the 8i and 8t, as “coming soon” on Google’s Cloud TPU page.

Delivering two newly introduced TPU systems nearly seven months after April’s pair shows Google wants to turn out specialized systems much more quickly than has been the case in the past. Now, it just needs to prove them, through benchmarks and an availability date when the hardware is actually in customers’ hands.

Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

#393. 'Sharp and futuristic': I rode Honda's first full-sized electric motorcycle

EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Techradar

'Sharp and futuristic': I rode Honda's first full-sized electric motorcycle

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1502 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Techradar

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Up until this point, the electric motorcycle industry has been largely dominated by a brace of brave startups, keen on proving that battery packs and electric motors make the perfect powertrain for a two-wheeler.
  • Maeving has been plowing ahead with its retro-inspired range of excellent city bikes, while Zero has been refining its line of adventure and performance machines for more than 20 years.
  • Harley-Davidson bucked the trend and was arguably the first major-name brand to put its reputation on the line, but sales haven’t exactly been going swimmingly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Up until this point, the electric motorcycle industry has been largely dominated by a brace of brave startups, keen on proving that battery packs and electric motors make the perfect powertrain for a two-wheeler.

Maeving has been plowing ahead with its retro-inspired range of excellent city bikes, while Zero has been refining its line of adventure and performance machines for more than 20 years.

Harley-Davidson bucked the trend and was arguably the first major-name brand to put its reputation on the line, but sales haven’t exactly been going swimmingly.

There are more names to mention, but the sector hasn't yet experienced anywhere near the sort of sales figures that electrified passenger vehicles have. Perhaps it is crying out for a more recognizable brand to get involved?

Now in steps Honda… one of the world’s most recognized automotive brands. After impressing with its CUV e electric scooter, it has decided to take things to the next level and release its first series-production, full-size electric motorcycle in the WN7. This could be just what the market needed.

Recent findings suggest that let’s deal with the name first, because it is, by far, one of the worst things about this machine. The ‘W’ apparently stands for ‘Wind,’ while the ‘N’ represents ‘Naked,’ as in it doesn’t have a fairing.

The seven? Well, that’s an indication of where it sits in the lineup, a bit like Kia’s EV naming strategy.

As is the way with many electric motorcycles, the WN7 can be specified in two power outputs: an 11kW A1-license-friendly version and an altogether more powerful 18kW version for those with a full A2 license.

Of course, licensing regulations differ throughout the world (apologies if you’re reading this from the US), but you get the idea. It can be purchased and ridden by people with a range of experience levels.

Even those with a more basic motorcycle license can experience some serious acceleration.

But the quirk of electric motorcycling is that both models have a peak power output of 50kW, or around 67bhp, and a hefty 100Nm of torque.

In other words, even those with a more basic motorcycle license can experience some serious acceleration.

In a recent development, the 9.3kWh lithium-ion battery is a 'stressed member', so the big block at the front essentially acts as part of the chassis. For this reason, the batteries aren’t removable, but it looks cool and makes the WN7 handle like a real sport bike.

In typical electric motorcycle fashion, there’s no clutch or gear lever to contend with. It’s just a case of twisting the throttle and hanging on.

The brakes, thankfully, are laid out like those on a traditional combustion motorcycle, with a lever mounted on the handlebar and a pedal by the right foot that controls the rear brake.

There’s a ‘tank,’ but it’s not filled with fuel. Instead, it houses the charging port, which can handle low-speed home charging as well as DC fast charging at public stations.

Honda states that using one of these, a 20% to 80% charge takes around 30 minutes. That’s enough for another 50 miles of riding in the time it takes to stretch the legs and an improvement on what Zero Motorcycles right now offers — although DC fast charging is promised for 2027.

Overall, Honda's claimed maximum range is 87 miles on a single charge, but, as you’ll see later, this is a tad unrealistic.

Sources indicate that firing up the WN7 is an interesting process. A remote key fob stays in your pocket, while a small ignition button on the frame turns everything on. From there, you pull in the brake lever, press a thumb switch on the handlebar, and it’s ready to go.

Recent findings suggest that cleverly, Honda has added forward and reverse assist, so it’s much easier to maneuver the 217kg machine at low speeds. Holding one of the corresponding buttons and gently twisting the throttle moves the bike backward or forward.

As you would expect from a Honda, everything immediately feels solid and well-built.

As you would expect from a Honda, everything immediately feels solid and well-built, while the decision to specify things like Showa inverted forks and large disc brakes with two-piston calipers up front inspires confidence.

The low center of gravity, aided by a whopping battery mounted low in the frame, makes it feel super stable, even at slow speeds.

Plus, the adjustable regenerative braking, accessed via paddles on the handlebar, makes it easy to set the amount of ‘engine braking’ the bike delivers.

This is important, because there’s nothing weirder than rolling off the throttle only for an electric motorcycle to coast almost forever. Adding a touch of regenerative braking means the bike slows as you ease off the throttle, which will feel far more natural for anyone used to combustion bikes.

Performance is strong and, like many larger electric motorcycles I have tested, the acceleration is almost sickeningly quick.

It has been revealed that A lack of gears makes the 0–60mph dash feel like being fired out of a cannon. Just pure torque and acceleration, before the WN7 runs out of puff at around 70mph.

According to recent reports, the bike is limited to 80mph, so it’s great for overtaking on slower country roads, but I found it a bit disconcerting when traffic started moving promptly. On highways, for example, where traffic flows at a steady 75mph, the WN7 feels underpowered.

But, perhaps more importantly, this feels like a proper Honda product. Much like the CUV e-scooter, the Japanese marque has put its stamp on a category that sometimes lacks finesse.

Aside from the uncomfortable seat, which looks like it has taken its color palette from a dentist’s chair, and the charging port, which likes to ping open with the mildest of touches, there’s a lot to like about the WN7 stylistically.

Industry observers note that it’s sharp, futuristic, and looks like very little else in the current Honda lineup. The massive TFT dash is ultra-bright and controlled via simple switchgear on the handlebar, although Honda has missed a trick by not adding true smartphone mirroring.

Instead, there’s a Honda RoadSync smartphone app that connects via Bluetooth and offers very simple navigation on the display, as well as music controls and some EV telemetry.

But pull over at an EV charging station and you’ll be accosted by bikers and electric car drivers alike. It’s a proper head-turner and conversation starter.

Get used to it, because you’ll be stopping at charging stations a lot (unless you tuck it away in a garage and sensibly charge overnight). The range is still just as much of an concern as it is with Honda’s rivals.

Industry observers note that the advertised 87 miles might be realistic if you simply use the bike for a quick dash across town, but the bike slurps juice like a thirsty Fortnite character anywhere else. During an admittedly very cold loan period, I watched the range drop in front of my eyes while enjoying the 60mph forest roads nearby.

During one day spent with it, when I captured the images for this feature, I probably covered around 50 miles on a full charge and managed to limp home with 5% battery remaining.

It feels cruel to get all this way and not mention the price. At £12,999 in the UK (around $17,200 / AU$25,300), the WN7 might be more expensive than similarly powerful Honda combustion bikes, but it’s very competitive compared to its electric rivals.

The Can-Am Pulse and LiveWire S2 are arguably its closest challengers, but Honda manages to hold its own with a mature ride, excellent build quality, and the all-crucial fast-charging technology.

Despite this, I couldn’t help coming away from my time with the bike wishing Honda — an engineering juggernaut — had done more.

According to recent reports, the WN7 still feels heavy, the range remains an glitch, and it’s not exactly shout-from-the-rooftops exciting to ride. There are just so many unforgettably visceral petrol bikes out there at this price.

But this feels like just the start, and if Honda gets cooking, we’re guaranteed to see an electric motorcycle that can finally hold its own against the combustion competition in the very near future.

Owners are reporting widely in the past few days that Live View video feeds from Nest Doorbells are broken in the Google Home app. The concern is affecting specifically the first-gen Nest Doorbell, which is best known as “Nest Hello,” but Google has been referring to it as “Nest Doorbell (wired, 1st gen).”.

The glitch has popped up in several Reddit threads in recent weeks, but seems to have spread much more widely in the past few days based on nearly a dozen Google support threads we found.

Some customers also report that some first-gen Nest cameras are also not working properly, but we couldn’t find nearly as many reports of this.

Notably, Google did roll out an revision to older Nest hardware at the end of October.

I'm so glad to see this article because I've been complaining and complaining to the void about this for weeks now. Google is taking NO responsibility to fix what they obviously broke. Internet searches say that I'm supposed to just upgrade the power supply but that makes no sense.

According to recent reports, interestingly, affected users say that Nest Doorbell notifications on Nest Hub displays are still working properly. Some have deduced that Google’s switch to WebRTC may be the cause of the problem, but it’s hard to say for certain seeing as workarounds based on that theory don’t reliably work.

According to recent reports, outside of generic troubleshooting messages, Google has yet to say anything about a fix, or even confirm there’s an concern. But, based on the number of reports, it’s very obvious there’s a problem on Google’s end.

We’ll patch this post as more details come to light but, for now, sound off in the comments below if you’re running into this issue.

Upgrade 11/7: Instead of pinned chats just appearing at the top of the list, Google Messages is trying a redesign that significantly elevates them above all conversations.

Hate the idea of just the pinned "bobble head" look. I like being able to view message tidbits. Plus, it's directly copying Apple (enough said). I have to use an iPhone at my job. I hate the pinned bubble conversation look and more importantly it's function.

These updates are at the moment in the beta channel and not yet widely rolled out to all testers. Some customers have all aspects of the redesign, but it appears that Google is rolling out the various components in a piecemeal fashion.
