#276. Google turned to AMD Epyc, not its own Axion chips, to secure its first confidential TPU

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1064 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Techradar

Google turned to AMD Epyc, not its own Axion chips, to secure its first confidential TPU

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1064 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Techradar

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google has added two more systems to its eighth-generation TPU family, and the one built for confidential AI leverages a host processor Google didn't design.
  • The TPU 8tx, detailed alongside the dual-chip TPU 8i Max in a Google Cloud blog post, pairs Google's accelerator silicon with 5th Gen AMD Epyc CPUs.
  • AMD also announced that Epyc forms the host foundation for what both companies call the first cloud TPU system with hardware-enforced confidential computing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google has added two more systems to its eighth-generation TPU family, and the one built for confidential AI leverages a host processor Google didn't design.

The TPU 8tx, detailed alongside the dual-chip TPU 8i Max in a Google Cloud blog post, pairs Google's accelerator silicon with 5th Gen AMD Epyc CPUs.

AMD also announced that Epyc forms the host foundation for what both companies call the first cloud TPU system with hardware-enforced confidential computing.

Recent findings suggest that google's April 2026 launch split its eighth generation hardware into the TPU 8t for training and the TPU 8i for inference. Google bills this as the first time it has introduced four TPU systems in one year, but as ServeTheHome points out, the two newcomers are system configurations built on existing chips rather than fresh designs.

As per Taiwanese outlet INSIDE, the 8tx inherits the 8t's 12.6 petaflops of FP4 compute and 216GB of HBM, but swaps in the lower-latency Boardfly network used by the 8i. Google claims up to 2x lower latency than TPU 8t with a near-zero performance penalty, and pitches the system at regulated enterprises and governments that want to fine-tune, distill, and train agents on private data without moving it between clusters.

Sources indicate that AMD indicates Epyc handles orchestration, data preparation, and the high-throughput link to the accelerators. Its Secure Encrypted Virtualization (SEV) works with the TPU to extend the protected environment out to the accelerators, checking each one's identity and security configuration before granting direct access to protected memory.

Sources indicate that prompts, model weights, and intermediate data stay encrypted in host memory and in transit, according to AMD, with hardware isolation while the TPU runs. Google, for its part, described the result as "keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use.".

Recent findings suggest that google hasn't directly said why it passed over Axion, the Neoverse V2-based chip it unveiled in 2024 as its first data center processor. Its own documentation offers a strong hint, however: Google's list of supported Confidential VM configurations runs entirely on AMD SEV and Intel TDX machines, with no Axion-based C4A or N4A instances, and states that TPUs can't right now be attached to Confidential VMs at all.

AMD's release adds that Google security experts have performed deep reviews of AMD's security processor firmware, and that SEV already underpins Google's Confidential VMs, Confidential GKE, Confidential Space, and confidential Spark and Dataflow services.

It could be argued here that confidential computing is only as credible as the years spent attacking it, and Google's audited chain of trust runs through x86. Building an equivalent on Axion would mean qualifying new hardware before shipping a product whose entire selling point is the "trust" it comes with, making it a moot point.

The move however is not a win for AMD's latest silicon; ServeTheHome reported that Google chose Turin to match the TPU 8t's PCIe Gen5 x16 interface, noting that a Gen6 host such as Venice would add no accelerator bandwidth, and tying the decision to Google's 2027 qualification schedule. Venice is AMD's 2nm flagship; the 8tx runs on a chip based on a family of CPUs that launched in October 2024.

Recent findings suggest that mark Lohmeyer, who runs AI and computing infrastructure at Google Cloud, told reporters that select customers will be able to deploy the 8tx in their own data centers, Data Center Knowledge reported, noting that Oracle recently noted it will offer TPUs on its cloud. INSIDE quoted Lohmeyer arguing that the technology lowers the risk of physical operators reaching sensitive data, even in third-party facilities.

According to recent reports, as TPUs spread beyond Google's own campuses, hardware attestation becomes the mechanism that lets a model owner place weights on hardware someone else runs. That interestingly puts AMD as a crucial part at the root of Google's off-campus trust offerings, a bigger role than the 8tx's niche positioning would initially suggest.

According to recent reports, it also revives August's rumor: A SemiAnalysis client note reported by Tom's Hardware, noted "Market chatter suggests [Google] is working with AMD on a TPU project in the v10 generation," possibly with CPU cores on the same package. The 8tx confirms neither claim as its Epyc chips sit in separate sockets, and nothing confirmed on November 9 involves AMD in accelerator design, but it does lend credence to potential future collaborations between the chip designer and the AI juggernaut.

The news saw AMD closing at $508.58 on November 9, up 13.26%, after trading as high as $515.18 on more than twice its recent average volume and while not all of it can be attributed to this particular development even as Oppenheimer's Rick Schafer upgraded AMD to Outperform with a $600 target, calling its server and data center success "undeniable", one could argue that it was a sizeable, if not the overwhelming catalyst in play that day.

The TPU 8tx arguably won't turn AMD's Epyc into a formidable TPU business overnight, and Google has left enough unpublished that its confidential computing claims deserve scrutiny once customers can test them.

However, one does need to account for the fact that when Google needed a host CPU to stake its first confidential TPU on, it picked AMD over its own chip, and that endorsement will outlast one day's share price increase as the latter aims to broaden its AI business even as its CEO recently branded the organization as "Data center-first" entity even as PC sales continue to plummet.

Keyboards are one of the most key, if not the most important, PC peripherals. You use your keyboard constantly — it's the primary input source for just about everyone (there are a few exceptions). And everyone deserves a keyboard that's a little nicer than the $5 board that was tossed in for free with your last PC purchase. Or — god forbid — whatever's built into your laptop.

Sources indicate that if you've got a gamer, a writer, or, well, anyone who uses a computer for any reason in your life, they could probably use a keyboard upgrade. Even keyboard enthusiasts with multiple mechanical boards will appreciate a upcoming one, especially if it fills a niche — say, a low-profile board that's portable and perfect for traveling, or a nostalgia-inducing retro-inspired board that's reminiscent of their favorite old-school game console.

It has been revealed that mechanical keyboards don't usually come cheap, but there are several budget-friendly boards that any keyboard lover would be thrilled to receive. And if they've already got the board of their dreams, pick up a fun accessory — a cool-looking cable, some pretty keycaps, or a wrist rest — to really elevate their typing experience.

Sources indicate that there aren't a ton of budget-friendly mechanical keyboards built for keyboard enthusiasts, but there are a few. These are all pre-built, so your recipient won't need to know how to assemble anything, but you can also often pick up bare-bones keyboard kits for cheaper than their fully built counterparts.

This full-size wired mechanical keyboard comes with red (linear) or brown (tactile) switches and has a hot-swappable PCB, PBT keycaps, and up to a 1,000 Hz polling rate — so it's great for both work and play.

Industry observers note that this compact 75% keyboard comes with Leobog Reaper switches, PBT keycaps, and a programmable knob. The shell is mostly plastic, but the layers of sound-dampening material make for a nice "thock.".

In a recent development, this 75% wireless mechanical keyboard features a gasket mount design, PBT keycaps, bright RGB backlighting, and a customizable TFT screen, as well as a programmable knob. And a hot-swappable PCB so you can bring your own switches.

Sources indicate that this low-profile wireless 75% mechanical keyboard comes with a wrist rest that doubles as a keyboard stand to adjust the angle. The board comes with low-profile linear switches and features a full aluminum body, so it looks and feels premium — but still costs under $100.

This 87-key Bluetooth/2.4GHz/USB keyboard has all the retro vibes of a classic IBM-style keyboard, but without the huge price tag! Kailh Box Switch V2 White mechanical key switches, dye-sub PBT keycaps, and multiple connection options make this a great keyboard for retro computing and getting work done.

An OG-Xbox-inspired 87-key keyboard with RGB backlight! You get 87 keys with Kailh Jellyfish X switches, double-layered ABS keycaps, and a lovely translucent green plastic shell! The colored cursor keys are beautiful.

If you're shopping for a keyboard enthusiast — or anyone who already has a keyboard they love, getting them a keyboard as a gift probably won't go over quite as well. But that doesn't mean you can't still pick up an accessory or two to complement their favorite board.

Sources indicate that cables are a part of life, but that doesn't mean they have to be ugly. This coiled USB-C cable from Keychron comes in four colors and is specifically designed to fit Keychron's K, K Pro, K Max, and K HE series boards, but will work with most USB-C boards. It comes with a 14cm coiled section and a 94cm straight cable that connect via a detachable aviator port, plus a USB-C to USB-A converter.

It has been revealed that not all keyboards have hot-swappable switches, but almost all of them have swappable keycaps. Glorious' cherry-profile keycaps are made of double-shot PBT and come in a variety of pretty, ombre colors.

In a recent development, just about every keyboard user could use a wrist rest, and this cooling gel-filled memory foam wrist rest from HyperX is one of our long-time favorites. It's durable and comfortable, and comes in multiple sizes to fit everything from compact to full-size keyboards.

Gel/foam wrist rests are comfortable, but wooden wrist rests are aesthetic (and comfortable, not everyone needs cushion under their wrists). This wooden wrist rest is designed to put your wrists in a neutral position and features non-slip feet to keep it from moving around. It comes in four sizes to fit everything from 60% to full-size keyboards.

  • The Korean tech giant announced today that preorders have now opened, but you’ll have to check if your phone is on the compatibility list to get a pair.
  • The idea with this collection is that it looks like regular eyewear, not another piece of conspicuous tech strapped to your face.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that samsung and Google are finally launching their Android XR smart glasses, as previously reported. The first collection pairs Samsung’s hardware prowess with designs from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker and will include 30 frame variations.

The Korean tech giant announced today that preorders have now opened, but you’ll have to check if your phone is on the compatibility list to get a pair.

The idea with this collection is that it looks like regular eyewear, not another piece of conspicuous tech strapped to your face. Gentle Monster has six different frame styles, each with a different lens treatment, whereas Warby Parker has three styles: Alden, Reid, and Wren.

Both collections come in various colors and prescription lens options. The glasses weigh around 41 grams, which is relatively lightweight for all-day wear, Samsung notes.

Industry observers note that the real attraction is more than just taking pictures without reaching for your phone. With Gemini in particular, you can identify landmarks, interpret unfamiliar objects, translate restaurant menus, and provide turn-by-turn directions through Google Maps. It can summarize meeting whiteboards and save the results to Samsung Notes.

Sources indicate that you interact with Gemini through voice commands or by tapping the frames. The glasses can also make phone calls, read out notifications, and help with day-to-day tasks. You get a 12MP HDR camera for photos and video, two open-ear speakers, and four mics.

Recent findings suggest that qualcomm’s Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 platform is the engine behind the experience, with up to nine hours of battery life. The included charging case provides up to seven additional charges.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

According to recent reports, warby Parker’s collection starts at $395, while Gentle Monster’s more premium frames start at $449 and go up to $489. That’s an affordable starting price compared to some rival smart glasses, but expect the final cost to be impacted by prescription options and individual frame choices.

Of course, when you start putting cameras and microphones on people’s faces, it raises some questions. Samsung claims there’s an external LED that should indicate when the camera is recording, with safeguards in place to prevent it from recording if someone covers the indicator or disables it. Gemini also automatically blurs faces of bystanders in visual requests. Google says it doesn't use visuals captured for AI training or ad targeting.

According to recent reports, there’s another catch, however: it’s not universally compatible. Supported devices are newer Samsung Galaxy phones running One UI 9 based on Android 17, Google Pixel 7 and later, and iPhone 13 Pro or later.

Preorders are now available through Google, Gentle Monster, and Warby Parker ahead of its December 10 launch in the US and South Korea (Gentle Monster models only).

#270. I’ve waited a long time for the Boox Picco, and I’m not disappointed

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1266 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5google

I’ve waited a long time for the Boox Picco, and I’m not disappointed

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1266 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At around $100, the Boox Picco offers one of the most portable e-reader experiences you can get.
  • There is an argument to be made for every single shape and size e-readers come in, and they come in so many different sizes it’s hard to keep track.
  • But even smaller devices like the Boox Palma make you choose between bringing a second device or sticking with your phone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At around $100, the Boox Picco offers one of the most portable e-reader experiences you can get. You add MagSafe-like capability with a refreshingly simple UI, and you have a delightful way to read, literally wherever you are.

There is an argument to be made for every single shape and size e-readers come in, and they come in so many different sizes it’s hard to keep track. I love the idea of having a 10-inch display that I can skim, but even if it’s perfect for sitting at home and reading anything from novels to comics, I don’t think it provides a very good travel experience.

But even smaller devices like the Boox Palma make you choose between bringing a second device or sticking with your phone. Most often, the phone wins out – especially when you have a flexible approach with a foldable like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 I’ve been using daily.

It has been revealed that unlike the other phone-sized e-readers from Boox, the Picco stands at just 4.15 inches tall. The screen measures at just under that – 3.97 inches. It’s essentially the size of a MagSafe or Qi2 wallet – just small enough to fit on the back of your phone with the included magnetic case.

Sources indicate that it’s thin, too. A 5.5mm side profile means it slips anywhere a minimal wallet would without matter. That goes for pockets just as well as crossbody bags; perfect for travel.

And that’s where I think I find so much more joy in using this over what would otherwise be considered a small e-reader, like the Palma. I don’t have a lot of excuses not to carry it around when I’m on the go. I’ll throw it in my Bellroy bag when I’m carrying what I’d considered my minimal EDC. It slides into any internal pocket, and it weighs next to nothing.

The back of the Boox Picco isn’t magnetic, but the included case is. If you want the thinnest possible footprint, forego the case. But adding it lets you do one of the coolest – and slightly copium-inducing – things with your phone: attach the e-ink device directly to your OLED-laden phone.

Recent findings suggest that it does not work well with an unconventional device like my Galaxy Z Fold 8, but if you have nearly any other device like the Pixel 11, you should get a rather perfect fit. The Picco squares up to the back of any slab phone with Qi2 magnets, whether internal or via a case.

But, why? Why slap another device and add weight/thickness to your phone when it’s perfectly capable of displaying e-books?

It has been revealed that because it’s cool! That’s the driving reason. You can make the argument that it doubles your phone’s usability or that it gives you an easy place to store the tiny e-reader. The truth is that it does add extra thickness to your phone, and using your phone with the Picco piggybacking along can be uncomfortable, since your fingers now rest on another display and not a case or phone backing.

You can get used to it, and, as unnecessary as it may seem, it’s a fun way to carry around a much more eye-friendly screen.

According to recent reports, the Picco diverts from other Boox devices in another way. It doesn’t run Android, which means you have no access to third-party apps like Google Play Books, Amazon Kindle, or any other store/library. Instead, the Picco uses a companion app to transfer EPUBs from your phone to the tiny e-reader.

Sources indicate that I initially opposed this idea when I got a sneak peek during IFA in Berlin this year. But after using it for a few weeks, I’ll admit I’ve come around. But that all comes down to how you consume your media.

It has been revealed that I try to source EPUBs no matter what device I use. On Android-powered e-readers, that means downloading Google Play Books and reading from there; I have my EPUBs uploaded to my own Google Play Books library, so they’re available universally.

According to recent reports, on the Picco, my approach hasn’t changed much. I take those same EPUBs I have in storage and transfer them from the companion app.

I can understand how the lack of third-party libraries would make the Boox Picco moot. Still, I’ve been a proponent of buying digital books I can store in my own drives, so I can read them wherever, whether that’s the Google Play Books library or from a device like the Picco.

All of that is a roundabout way of saying the Picco, though it doesn’t let you use apps to read, makes it easy to get digital copies loaded and ready to flip through.

It has been revealed that it uses a handshake connection that requires you to open the companion app on your phone, hit connect, and do the same on the Picco. Once connected, transferring EPUB files is as easy as selecting them from your phone’s physical or cloud storage and queueing them up. The process takes seconds, and the only problem I’ve had was solved by a force stop and trying again.

Industry observers note that the homescreen is simply a carousel of your library, with a delightful little progress bar under each title as they’re sorted. You can access and manage the bookshelf from that page, as well as the minimal “apps” and settings. I appreciate the focus app and reading stats, but the countdown and to-do options require using the companion app. I don’t see the point of those.

It doesn’t even have a control panel. Swiping down from the top surfaces screen brightness and color controls. Even though this little guy is just over $100, it still has a front light controlled by a physical switch on the side. Compare that to e-readers at much higher price points without that game-changing feature.

It has been revealed that the buttons opposite don’t control volume. Instead, they’re there for page turning.

It’s just simple and well-designed. Features are there to make reading a better experience, down to granular text controls for your digital books. It does exactly what it needs to do – nothing more, nothing less.

It has been revealed that as far as battery goes, it meets my expectations. It’s not massive, so the battery is small in comparison to a smartphone. It still holds its own easily, with an easy week of use if you’re reading for an hour or two a day. Beyond that, it takes little time to charge and does great on idle, which is perfect for such a passive device.

The Picco will hit home for you if you want an ultra-portable option for your e-books. The same goes for those who don’t mind the smaller screen and lack of Android or third-party app support.

I get genuine joy every time I pick it up to read where I left off, and I think that’s because it’s so simple and nothing about it feels bloated, even the companion app, which is also straight to the point.

Industry observers note that I think it’s been a while since a device has offered that experience for me. Adding the form factor, optional magnetic attachment for your phone, and price tag just gets me to that conclusion sooner.

The Boox Picco is the most adorable e-reader I’ve used, and it’s $109 on Amazon.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, nvidia's board of directors has approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas as a potential successor to Jensen Huang, according to a report from the Financial Times that cites people familiar with the matter.
  • Recent findings suggest that the search for Nvidia's next chief executive comes as the company undergoes a leadership transition following Jensen Huang's swift departure from the CEO position earlier this week.
  • Rene Haas is no stranger to Nvidia, as he spent approximately seven years at the manufacturer before leaving in 2013.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, nvidia's board of directors has approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas as a potential successor to Jensen Huang, according to a report from the Financial Times that cites people familiar with the matter. Haas is among several candidates under consideration, although it remains unclear whether he will get a formal offer and/or agree to take the position.

Recent findings suggest that the search for Nvidia's next chief executive comes as the company undergoes a leadership transition following Jensen Huang's swift departure from the CEO position earlier this week. For now, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress serves as interim CEO. The company's board is currently searching for a permanent replacement and is reportedly evaluating both internal and external candidates. Neither Arm nor Nvidia commented on the matter to FT.

Rene Haas is no stranger to Nvidia, as he spent approximately seven years at the manufacturer before leaving in 2013. During his tenure as vice president at Nvidia, he was responsible for multiple projects, including notebook GPUs, Windows-on-Arm, and Tegra system-on-chips. Given that he held senior management positions, he certainly gained experience with Nvidia's operations, corporate culture, and relationships with customers and partners.

Furthermore, Haas has experience with the development of consumer and data center CPUs as well as GPUs and GPU IP, a combination that is hard to find in the industry. Haas reportedly maintains close ties with Jensen Huang and several members of Nvidia's board, which could make him a particularly attractive candidate for a organization whose strategy and management structure have orbited around its founder for more than three decades.

While at Arm, Haas has demonstrated a willingness to make substantial strategic changes at the firm. Since Haas took the reins in 2022, Arm has introduced its Compute Subsystems (CSS) initiative, providing customers with complete and validated processor platform design, making it easier for newcomers to enter the market. Arm also introduced its first own-brand AGI CPU, putting the company in direct competition with some of its traditional customers. Both initiatives represent significant departures from Arm's traditional business model; however, they demonstrate Haas' readiness to pursue latest revenue opportunities despite risks and the possibility of damaging relationships with long-term partners.

Sources indicate that another advantage is Haas' extensive experience with the semiconductor industry in general. Arm's CPU and GPU technologies are used in system-on-chips developed by hundreds of companies that have very distinctive requirements, including Nvidia itself, Apple, Qualcomm, and MediaTek, just to name a few.

It has been revealed that in addition, Haas led Arm through its initial public offering in 2023 and therefore has experience with investors and regulators. Also, Haas happens to be the CEO of SoftBank, the parent of Arm.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

In a recent development, nevertheless, Haas' potential appointment would not be without challenges, primarily because he has never managed a company the scale of Nvidia. Arm has around 10,000 employees worldwide; it develops and licenses various semiconductor IP, primarily CPU and GPU technologies, to a wide range of customers with distinct needs. By contrast, Nvidia designs CPUs, GPUs, networking equipment, complete AI systems, and software platforms and has a headcount of about 42,000. As a result, if Haas becomes the boss of Nvidia, he will have to manage a considerably bigger organization with a dramatically more complicated product portfolio and supply chain. Furthermore, replacing Huang, who has led Nvidia since its establishment in 1993 and personally shaped its technology strategy and business tactics, would be a formidable task for virtually any executive.

Ironically, Haas' appointment (if it happens) would create an unusual situation in which Nvidia will be led by the chief executive of a firm it attempted to acquire in 2020 and abandoned the transaction in 2022 amid regulatory opposition.

However, Samsung also wants to collaborate with established medical institutions in South Korea. The goal is to standardize health data available through the Samsung Health app to deliver greater value to users. There's still a long road ahead for Samsung and its partner institutions, as the post says the company is working on (and providing) proofs of concept with hospitals.

Recent findings suggest that in the U.S., Choi says Samsung wants to leverage its acquisition of Xealth. Xealth excels in digital health solutions for hospitals. It reduces the gap between the health data you capture on a Galaxy Watch and what your doctor sees and knows about you. Samsung says it wants to pursue deeper partnerships with U.S. hospitals through Xealth by 2030, potentially connecting consumers with over 100 institutions.

Samsung continues to push for better health assistance and insights, and I think this is totally worth it. If we're going to use AI to help, this is where it should be applied. It's even more worth it when you consider that your data will be shared with your hospital. This gets your doctor's eyes on your info, and they can make the judgment call that truly matters. ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly accepted kernel patch slated for the upcoming Linux 7.5 release finally resolves a long-standing hardware video decoding bug on AMD's ancient R600 architecture, nearly two decades after the cards first hit store shelves.
  • Sources indicate that I investigated video corruption on my older iMac7,1 (RV610/M74, device ID 1002:94c8).
  • According to recent reports, interestingly, the breakthrough didn't come from a grizzled veteran of the open-source graphics stack, but from a newcomer utilizing OpenAI's Codex to help untangle the legacy driver path.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly accepted kernel patch slated for the upcoming Linux 7.5 release finally resolves a long-standing hardware video decoding bug on AMD's ancient R600 architecture, nearly two decades after the cards first hit store shelves. As spotted by Phoronix, the fix targets the Unified Video Decoder (UVD) engine across the RV610, RV620, RV630, RV635, and RV670 silicon families, making up the Radeon HD 2000 and HD 3000 families released starting in 2007. Linux users running these cards experienced visual corruption during hardware-accelerated video playback whenever the GPU was simultaneously handling active 3D or desktop drawing workloads; those issues should now be resolved.

Sources indicate that I investigated video corruption on my older iMac7,1 (RV610/M74, device ID 1002:94c8). When the decoder was reading compressed video from system memory while the GPU was drawing, it would corrupt video frames. Moving the input to VRAM allowed frames to decode correctly. Disabling graphics draws also stopped the corruption. Here is a proposal to keep UVD buffers in VRAM for this family of devices, as the driver already does for some other chips. The patch covers RV610, RV620, RV630, RV635 and RV670. These chips share the RV6xx decoder path and legacy R600 firmware, so I think they are likely to have the same hardware requirements. Someone with the other hardware would need to verify that. I tested this on Debian. I used Codex to help with the investigation, testing and patch.

According to recent reports, interestingly, the breakthrough didn't come from a grizzled veteran of the open-source graphics stack, but from a newcomer utilizing OpenAI's Codex to help untangle the legacy driver path. The culprit turned out to be a memory placement oversight: the driver wasn't consistently keeping UVD input buffers pinned inside dedicated VRAM. When graphics draw calls competed for resources, frames failed to decode properly. By forcing those buffers to stay in VRAM — a behavior the Radeon kernel driver apparently already enforced for several other chip families — video playback cleans right up.

According to recent reports, it is easy to forget just how pivotal the R600 generation was for PC graphics. Launching in 2007 as the first desktop GPU lineup built under the AMD banner following that firm's blockbuster acquisition of the Canadian ATI Technologies Inc., the Radeon HD 2000 series marked the fresh AMD graphics division's transition away from separate pixel and vertex pipelines on the desktop, after implementing the tech first for the Xbox 360. The move to a unified shader architecture arrived alongside DirectX 10 and Windows Vista, so it was a time of many transitions.

In a recent development, while the flagship Radeon HD 2900 XT famously struggled against Nvidia's dominant GeForce 8800 GTX in raw gaming rasterization and power draw, the R600 family brought serious multimedia chops to the table. The introduction of the first-generation Unified Video Decoder (UVD) on the mainstream RV610 and RV630 chips, and later the refined RV670 powering the beloved Radeon HD 3850 and 3870, allowed even budget PCs to offload heavy H.264 and VC-1 Blu-ray decoding from the CPU. In 2007, smooth 1080p playback without maxing out a dual-core processor was a major selling point for many owners, but none more so than home theater PC (HTPC) builders.

It has been revealed that of course, almost nobody is daily driving a TeraScale 1 graphics card in 2026, especially when modern integrated graphics run circles around them at a fraction of the wattage; the contributor who submitted the patches wants them for his ancient Core 2 Duo-based iMac. Yet, there is something quietly heartwarming about the longevity of open-source Linux drivers. Whereas proprietary Windows support for the HD 2000 and 3000 series was sunsetted over a decade ago, the mainline Linux kernel continues to carry the torch. Combined with recent AI-assisted cleanup efforts across the Mesa R600 user-space driver, vintage Radeon hardware is arguably in better software shape today than it was during its actual retail lifespan.

The tech giant has revealed that automated server health checks misfired, kicking healthy infrastructure offline and triggering cascading connection failures across Exchange Online, Teams, and Copilot. Instead, a particular server component that does those checks started failing its own tests. Over a hundred thousand frustrated users were left with broken inboxes and unable to get work done as Microsoft Outlook went down on Thursday, November 12.

Outlook users in the Americas began reporting they could not access their Exchange Online mailboxes, and the complaints were rolling in fast, with Downdetector reporting more than 125,000 complaints as of this writing.

If you attempted to refresh your inbox only to be greeted by infinite loading screens, you were not the only one. The problem is due to the way Outlook clients authenticate and connect to Exchange Online mailboxes using different connection methods.

Microsoft engineers are currently scrambling to resolve problems on the server end and mitigate the impact, but the tech giant has not yet provided a concrete timeline for a full fix.

Apps in Microsoft 365 that rely on the same service connectivity may also be slow or throw error codes until the dust settles, though Exchange Online takes the biggest hit. According to recent reports, "Luckily there is a huge catalogue of music, film and novels to dive into, and we took inspiration from all of them, as well as other sources not in the Bond world," Henson noted. "So many great composers have added their voice to the franchise, from John Barry to Eric Serra, Michael Kamen to Hans Zimmer, and it is fascinating to hear how each one approaches the material," the composer said.

#258. Technical Debt is Social; it is the Price of Learning by Doing

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (832 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Infoq

Technical Debt is Social; it is the Price of Learning by Doing

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (832 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Technical Debt is Social; it is the Price of Learning by Doing.
  • Nov 12, 2026 3 min read.
  • Sources indicate that technical debt is not necessarily a sign of poor engineering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Technical Debt is Social; it is the Price of Learning by Doing.

Nov 12, 2026 3 min read.

Sources indicate that technical debt is not necessarily a sign of poor engineering. It can be the price of learning through software in use. As AI accelerates code production beyond our capacity to understand code and context, technical debt increasingly becomes a sociotechnical challenge, Xin Yao noted in her talk "What If Your Biggest Technical Debt Is Social", at GOTO Copenhagen.

Yao quoted Ward Cunningham, who defined debt as "not-quite-right code". Debt sounds like a negative thing, but it can be a deliberate business strategy, she explained:.

If we release the code now, well knowing it’s not perfect for the future yet, we’ll get some business feedback, we’ll get some user feedback, we’ll probably get paid for something, and that’s good as a business strategy.

Industry observers note that debt isn’t about poorly written code; it arises when we design software with incomplete knowledge. Hence, debt is the price of learning by doing, Yao argued. Releasing software allows us to test our assumptions against reality. Once we’ve got a learning experience, we have to put that experience back into our code and pay off the debt, she added. The debt becomes problematic when our software doesn’t catch up with our upcoming learning.

Sources indicate that debt can be a good communication strategy toward management. It provides an economic argument for the cost of postponing architectural improvements. However, framing technical debt solely as something to eliminate misses its strategic value. The question is not whether to incur debt, but whether the learning it enables justifies the cost, and whether we actually repay it.

It has been revealed that yao referred to Kent Beck’s article "Earn and Learn," which explores features vs. futures. Features deliver value today, while the future is actually the optionality to adapt those features, Yao explained:.

Recent findings suggest that every bit of code already coded is complexity and a constraint. Every feature removes some future. If you go on producing features, maybe using your LLMs, then at a certain point, all you can do is use your capacity to pay the interest, to fix the code, and you can no longer release features.

The challenge is to balance delivering features with preserving future options, Yao remarked. Sometimes, delaying a design commitment preserves options until we know more, and this includes postponing some upfront architecture decisions to the last responsible moment as well. As Beck argues, waiting is not laziness; waiting is holding an asset.

According to recent reports, technical debt can therefore be understood as learning made visible in software. We design based on what we know, observe software’s impact, modularity, and its architecture’s implications, and we enhancement our understanding, Yao explained:.

The software no longer fits what we now understand, and yesterday’s good understanding becomes today’s debt.

AI introduces a new challenge: software can now be produced faster than teams can develop a shared understanding of its behavior, design decisions and consequences, Yao argued.

Agentic coding makes debt repayment more complex; beyond addressing poorly written AI-generated code, teams must close the gap between what the software actually does and what they understand it to do, while ensuring the code keeps pace with their evolving domain and architectural understanding. Paying off debt is no longer just a technical task, but a sociotechnical one, Yao concluded.

InfoQ interviewed Xin Yao after her talk.

InfoQ: What does learning from technical debt look like, and what benefit does it bring?

Xin Yao: We design and release software based on our best current understanding, then test our assumptions against business and user reality. Paying off debt means incorporating that learning back into the software and closing the gap between what we knew when we released the first iteration and what we know now.

Each iteration creates new debt and new learning. Small batches and tight feedback loops help teams retain the memory of their initial design decisions and continuously repay the old debt with new learning.

InfoQ: What does technical debt look like now that developers are using artificial intelligence?

Industry observers note that yao: With agentic coding, software production can outpace human understanding. Code increasingly becomes a fossil record of agents’ decisions, while humans remain accountable for its consequences. Local productivity gains can create collective costs: more code, weaker ownership and growing gaps in shared understanding.

Industry observers note that A study on How Developers Discuss the Burden of AI-Assisted Software Development describes this as "a tragedy of the commons". The danger is not merely more poorly written agentic code, but accelerated learning debt across the sociotechnical system.

#256. Samsung’s Smart Glasses Won’t Let You Live Stream to Social Media

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (505 w)
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Androidheadlines

Samsung’s Smart Glasses Won’t Let You Live Stream to Social Media

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (505 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidheadlines

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google’s latest privacy rules block apps on Samsung Intelligent Eyewear from social live streaming, something Ray-Ban Meta glasses can do.
  • Recent findings suggest that samsung’s smart glasses won’t let you go live on social media, and that’s by design.
  • Shahram Izadi, Google’s VP and GM of XR, detailed the protections in a blog post on November 12, as SamMobile points out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s latest privacy rules block apps on Samsung Intelligent Eyewear from social live streaming, something Ray-Ban Meta glasses can do. The glasses also detect a covered recording light, blur bystanders’ faces before sending images to Gemini, and keep camera data out of AI training. They’re up for pre-order now and ship in mid-December.

Recent findings suggest that samsung’s smart glasses won’t let you go live on social media, and that’s by design. Google indicates its Play Store rules block apps from using the camera on Intelligent Eyewear for social live streaming, which sets these glasses apart from Meta’s. It’s one of several privacy rules Google laid out just as the glasses opened for pre-order this week, and they’re meant to pair with the Android phones you already have.

Shahram Izadi, Google’s VP and GM of XR, detailed the protections in a blog post on November 12, as SamMobile points out. He said privacy on glasses has to protect both the person wearing them and the people in front of them.

Google Play’s policies now bar apps from social live streaming, real-time facial recognition, and changing how the outward recording light works. That’s a substantial difference from Ray-Ban Meta glasses, which can stream straight to Instagram and Facebook.

Every pair has an outward-facing light that turns on when you take a photo or record video. If you cover it or tamper with it, sensors are designed to notice and block the camera. Google indicates this light was the feature bystanders found most helpful in its testing.

The glasses are also designed to blur the faces of people around you before an image gets sent to Gemini. The microphones focus on your voice by default, not the conversations around you. There’s also a physical switch to turn the glasses off completely.

Google states what the camera sees isn’t used to train its AI models or to target ads, and it isn’t saved in your Gemini history. Data on the glasses is encrypted, and so is anything sent to your phone or the cloud. Third-party apps have to ask permission before they can use the camera, and you can revoke that access at any time.

The rules extend to the people wearing them. To use the glasses, you have to agree not to record people without permission, not to record in sensitive places, and not to cover the light. Breaking those rules can get your glasses disabled. Setup also requires a Google account for someone 18 or older.

Google’s timing makes sense. Meta has been under pressure for months over how its glasses get used, including a letter from Senators Ron Wyden and Ed Markey asking about LED tampering and footage of people recorded without their consent. Google is clearly trying to get ahead of those questions before its glasses ship.

Samsung Intelligent Eyewear runs Android XR and opened for pre-order on November 12 through Warby Parker and Gentle Monster, with deliveries expected in mid-December. It releases first in the US and South Korea.

  • Adam Turaj, a Mechatronics Engineering student at the University of Waterloo, built an open-source LEGO 3D printer named “Studprint” with only 13 pieces of the printer not made out of LEGO.
  • According to recent reports, earlier this year, Hack Club posted a challenge called Infill, calling makers and hobbyists to design their own 3D printers from scratch and receive a $350 grant to build their printers.
  • It has been revealed that turaj joined this challenge, designing his LEGO 3D printer in SOLIDWORKS.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Adam Turaj, a Mechatronics Engineering student at the University of Waterloo, built an open-source LEGO 3D printer named “Studprint” with only 13 pieces of the printer not made out of LEGO. The bill of materials only totals $173.35, with $30 of the budget going to LEGO pieces that comprise 92% of the whole build. Turaj’s project got him flown to the Rocky Mountain RepRap Festival 2026, where he got to meet Prusa CMO Zack Freedman and presented Studprint to over 4,000 people at the event.

According to recent reports, earlier this year, Hack Club posted a challenge called Infill, calling makers and hobbyists to design their own 3D printers from scratch and receive a $350 grant to build their printers. Whoever submits a benchy with their printer gets a chance to be flown to the Rocky Mountain RepRap Festival 2026, and Turaj was one of them.

It has been revealed that turaj joined this challenge, designing his LEGO 3D printer in SOLIDWORKS. He named the project Studprint, referring to the studs on a LEGO brick. What takes this project even farther is that Turaj decided he would only use “classical LEGO,” avoiding LEGO Technic pieces wherever possible. Looking at the repository’s images of the CAD designs, you would easily mistake it for a virtual LEGO builder.

Turaj shared an image of the bill of materials (BOM) on the GitHub repository for his build, showing a final build price of $173.35. There are three major electronics components in the printer: the first is the BTT SKR Pico V1.0, a control board commonly used in open-source 3D printers like the Voron V0; for wireless capability, a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W is used; and the whole printer is powered by a Mean Well LRS-150-24 switching power supply — with all three components priced at around $25 each. This printer is built with the backbone of a true DIY 3D-printer build, unlike this cute LEGO 3D printer we covered last year that used a 3D printing pen.

In a recent development, there are five NEMA 17 stepper motors, also popular in 3D printers, whether open- or closed-source. Four of the motors control the axes, while the fifth is used to feed filament to the Trianglelab V6 Extruder. The rest of the 3D printer is made of $30 worth of LEGO pieces; even the build plate is a block of LEGO. Turaj’s only print shown on the GitHub repository is a Benchy, sliced in Klipper and printed in 1.25 hours; it’s surprisingly good considering the leadscrews are all LEGO pieces.

#251. Today I learned why wind farms paint one turbine blade black

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (651 w)
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Techradar

Today I learned why wind farms paint one turbine blade black

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (651 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Techradar

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You'd think that painting a single turbine blade black is a pretty inexpensive fix for accidental bird deaths.
  • Sources indicate that at the Smøla wind farm in Norway, every wind turbine had one of its blade painted black for an extended science experiment back in August 2013.
  • However, similar experiments in the Netherlands did not yield positive results, because apparently this fix depends heavily on the local bird species and population size.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You'd think that painting a single turbine blade black is a pretty inexpensive fix for accidental bird deaths. It sounds almost too good to be true, which perhaps it is.

Sources indicate that at the Smøla wind farm in Norway, every wind turbine had one of its blade painted black for an extended science experiment back in August 2013. Over the next three years, the number of bird carcasses found fell by 70%.

However, similar experiments in the Netherlands did not yield positive results, because apparently this fix depends heavily on the local bird species and population size.

It has been revealed that there are a total of 68 turbines at the Smøla wind power plant, an archipelago off the coast of Central Norway. Researchers from the Norwegian Institute for Nature Research compared four regular turbines with four neighboring ones that had one blade painted black for this experiment.

They regularly counted the number of bird carcasses within 100 meters of the wind farm. This continued over a period of more than ten years, combining 7.5 years of baseline data from before painting any turbine blades to 3.5 years of data from after. In 2020, they published their findings in a paper called Ecology and Evolution.

In a recent development, turns out that this small change in visual cues reduced the number of bird deaths by over 70%, proving especially effective on the somewhat rare white-tailed sea eagle population of the region. While the researchers noted that this anecdotal data may not hold up to different bird populations, this was still independent real-world confirmation of a separate laboratory experiment that found similar results in 2003.

Recent findings suggest that what difference does one black blade make? According to researchers, it has to do with how birds process visual cues.

Animation designers call it motion smearing, where images that move too fast for the human eye to follow are inferred in the brain as one continuous motion. When turbine blades are in motion, birds find it difficult to notice the threat because the unicolor rotating blades look like one giant circle.

When you paint one of these blades black, it breaks up the pattern so the moving blades are more easily distinguishable to the eye. But as Audubon reported, these are preliminary findings that won't translate to all bird species equally — especially ones that don't have the visual acuity to notice the difference. There's also a significant amount of effort involved, since painting turbines in operation requires both lifts and specialist crews who can navigate the height.

Most of the land experiments so far have stuck with black, but at sea, a newly introduced trial is experimenting with a different color.

Recent findings suggest that dutch consortium Ecowende is fitting seven Vestas V236-15.0 MW turbines with one red 115.5-meter blade each. Red was chosen after weighing options against criteria such as durability and heat management, apart from the obvious benefit of being more easily discernible from a distance.

In a recent development, that remarked, seabirds may generally need less help than expected. A Vattenfall and Spoor study at its Aberdeen offshore wind farm tracked 2,007 flight paths over 19 months. It found no confirmed collisions, with birds typically keeping 100 to 200 meters away.

Industry observers note that dropbox built what it calls "an auditor for our auditor," a companion URL detector that uses traffic data to find every live Dropbox web surface. Billions of visit records are filtered down to a manageable list of unique paths, then grouped by consent logic so that representative URLs can stand in for large families of similar pages.

Platform engineers interested in building similar tooling can see the shape of a minimal Playwright assertion in a recent qaskills.sh guide.

Sources indicate that today the auditor produces a weekly report for Privacy and Engineering teams, separating likely violations from known false positives and tracking historical trends. Dropbox's next planned iteration is routing findings directly to the teams that own each page, shortening the loop between detection and fix. The team notes that the browser automation itself may be the simplest part of such a project, with the harder work sitting around it: defining correct behaviour, maintaining an accurate inventory and separating real issues from noise.

Dropbox is a cloud-based file hosting and collaboration platform founded in 2007 by Drew Houston and Arash Ferdowsi and headquartered in San Francisco. The company operates more than 200 web surfaces across its product lineup, which includes Dropbox, Dropbox Sign, DocSend and FormSwift, and has invested heavily in privacy and compliance programmes covering GDPR, CCPA and ISO 27018.

According to recent reports, playwright is an open-source browser automation library developed and maintained by Microsoft. It drives Chromium, WebKit and Firefox through a single API across JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java and .NET, and has become a widely used tool for end-to-end testing, web scraping and, increasingly, automated privacy and compliance audits of the kind Dropbox describes.

Peacock’s mobile app is about to look a lot more like TikTok. NBCUniversal is testing a redesign with a vertical video feed and AI-powered search, calling it its biggest mobile upgrade yet.

Sources indicate that NBCUniversal unveiled the redesigned app on November 11, as Android Central reports. Peacock has already started testing the latest features and plans to keep testing them into 2027, so there’s no firm date for when everyone gets them.

In a recent development, the headline feature is the Clips Feed, a vertical video section for finding indicates, movies, and sports. It lives in its own tab, so you won’t have to scroll through it to get to the regular home screen. Peacock states vertical video is central to making the mobile app feel different from what you see on your TV.

Sources indicate that search is getting a Gemini-style makeover. Along with searching by title, you’ll be able to describe a mood or theme, then narrow down the results by continuing the conversation. Think “something funny and short for tonight,” then “only comedies with a reality TV vibe.”.

Recent findings suggest that peacock is also adding Franchise Hubs for its biggest indicates and series. They’ll pull together episodes, podcasts, interactive games, and live moments in one place. Minions, Love Island USA, and The Traitors are among the first examples.

It has been revealed that jim Denney, Peacock’s chief product officer, said the goal is for Peacock to be more than a place to watch. He described it as an entertainment platform that helps fans find and engage with content they love.

It has been revealed that peacock is following a trend here. Netflix has already added its own vertical video feed, and Spotify has added short-form video in its app. Android Central’s Rowan Davies isn’t a fan, arguing these feeds are mostly built to keep you in the app longer, not to help you find something to watch. I agree with that. I want to open a streaming app, pick a show, and start watching. I don’t need another feed to scroll before bed.

Sources indicate that still, it’s easy to see why Peacock wants this. It held 2.6% of all US TV viewing in Nielsen’s July report, well behind YouTube and Netflix, and streaming has become a fight for attention. A feed that keeps people in the app longer is one way to compete, whether viewers asked for it or not.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang was one of the American success stories in Silicon Valley, where he had his humble beginnings as a seasonal dishwasher, busboy, and waiter at his nearby Denny’s before he rose to stardom as the head of Nvidia. The diner honored this achievement with a plaque at the booth where Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem met after their working hours and first planned the inception of Nvidia. However, NBC News mentioned that the sign has since been removed following Huang’s spectacular fall from grace and resignation from the tech giant.

Sources indicate that unfortunately, employees say that the commemorative plaque, which read, “The booth that launched a $1 trillion manufacturer,” has been removed. It remains unclear who ordered the removal, though, so we reached out to Denny’s for comment and will patch the story if they answer.

Despite being a billionaire, the former Nvidia CEO is known for keeping in touch with his roots. He has been spotted several times eating street food and enjoying local fast food in the various cities that he visits. He even once dragged the 35 Taiwanese industry chiefs to a restaurant in Taipei, earning that event the moniker “trillion-dollar banquet.” This “man of the people” persona has made him quite a popular figure among some people, fueling the Jensanity hype, especially in his home country of Taiwan.

We also saw this side of Jensen during the unveiling of the plaque in 2023, after Nvidia hit a $1 trillion valuation, when he balanced 10 plates and served food during the event. The restaurant also put up a food truck and served “Nvidia Breakfast Bytes” at GTC 2025, which consisted of four sausage links served with four buttermilk silver dollar pancakes and some syrup, and was available for a limited time for under $5 in all Denny’s branches across the country.

Sources indicate that this move is just another sign of Jensen’s sudden downfall. He was still the leader of one of the most valuable companies in the world a couple of weeks ago, evangelizing artificial intelligence to anyone willing to listen. Today finds a totally different reality, with sources saying that he looked “broken and shattered,” and he even called himself “a piece of sh--” as he left the tech giant he built for over 30 years after the board ousted him.

There is no telling yet what’s next for Jensen Huang. Elon Musk has reportedly offered him a position, saying that it “would be an honor” to hire the person who was arguably one of the biggest driving forces in today’s AI industry, but he’s also facing numerous investigations from both his company, Congress, and the FBI. More importantly, Jensen will have to deal with the fallout of the revelations on his public image and personal life.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With Google’s Pixel Tag now offiically available, Google has also confirmed where the Android Find Hub tracker will be on sale, and it’s a limited list.

In a recent development, compared to the two dozen countries where Pixel 11 phones and the Pixel Watch 5 are sold, the Pixel Tag tracker is only being sold in 8 countries at launch. This could change over time, but that’s all that Google is officially supporting for the time being, as detailed on a support page.

That country exclusion is really odd, given that (aside from Singapore and India, where Pixel Tag is sold), the main European Union countries are the only places where Android has a stronger market share majority over iOS, hence leading to a much better Find Hub network.

India: Android 94.8% - iOS 5.1%.

European Union: Android ~64.0% - iOS ~36.0%.

Singapore: Android 57.5% - iOS 42.4%.

United Kingdom: Android 49.3% - iOS 50.4%.

Taiwan: Android 48.4% - iOS 51.6%.

Japan: Android 46.2% - iOS 53.8%.

United States: Android 40.1% - iOS 59.7%.

Australia: Android 38.4% - iOS 61.3%.

Canada: Android 36.6% - iOS 63.3%.

(courtesy of Gemini Argon - I've used my weekly quota for you haha).

Countries where Pixel Tag will be sold include:.

According to recent reports, does this mean that Pixel Tag won’t work in countries where it’s not sold? There’s no definitive answer on that yet, but it likely will at least function – travel is one of the biggest places a tracker like this is used, after all. Buyers in other countries, though, may not be able to buy it from authorized retailers and won’t be able to use Google’s warranty if they obtained it elsewhere.

Google may end up expanding the list of countries where Pixel Tag is sold in time, of course. A very obvious gap here is Europe, where Pixel Tag simply isn’t sold (aside from the United Kingdom, which is part of Europe as a region, but not a part of the European Union).

Recent findings suggest that google’s newly introduced Pixel Feature Drop enhancement, the one for November 2026, brought forth two complications for Pixel devices. The update is essentially breaking Pixel cameras and wireless charging.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A Chinese military medical school has just developed a UAV that could remotely administer medicine, helping treat injured soldiers on the front lines without putting medical personnel at risk. According to Chinese mouthpiece Global Times, the Air Force Medical University built the first casualty-search drone for the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) that fires darts loaded with painkillers to help ease the pain of wounded personnel.

“We have developed the military’s first casualty-search drone and have also made some breakthroughs in treatment. For example, we can use drones to inject medication into wounded personnel from a considerable distance,” Air Force Medical University representative Wang Jianqi told the publication. “Wherever our drone can fly, we can deliver life-saving emergency medication into a wounded person’s muscle, buying valuable time for treatment.”.

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine saw the widespread use of drones on the frontline, primarily for search-and-destroy and reconnaissance missions. However, the four-year escalation of the 12-year war has seen the creative implementations of these units — from jam-proof fiber optic drones to the use of heavy-lift hexacopters for medical evacuation. Now, drones-as-first-responders are being developed for civilian use, including firefighting drones, camera response drones, and even “Campus Guardian Angel” drones designed to neutralize school shooters.

However, China's air-ground treatment drone remains in the experimental stage, notes Wang. After all, you can’t just administer medication without assessing the patient’s vital signs and their injuries. It’s also difficult or even impossible to load an incapacitated soldier without external assistance. Still, the deployment of medical UAVs would help with battlefield medicine, which has developed the concept of the “golden hour,” which suggests that wounded personnel treated within the first hour have the greatest chance of survival.

Industry observers note that although battlefield medicine was in use since the 1800s, especially during Napoleon’s invasion of Russia and the American Civil War, helicopter medevacs were first deployed during World War 2 in Burma and the Philippines. The Korean War saw the introduction of MASH — Mobile Army Surgical Hospital — units that brought forward treatment units closer to the frontline.

This, combined with the widespread use of UH-1 Hueys during the Vietnam War to evacuate wounded soldiers from the front lines, sometimes while under enemy fire, has greatly increased the survival rate among wounded soldiers. Today, helicopter and ground medevacs are common among military forces, with drone treatment and evacuation now being experimented with in both the frontlines of Ukraine and military medical universities in China.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Original Mass Effect composer Jack Wall has recalled working on BioWare's role-playing game (RPG), describing the collaborative project as a "rewarding" experience that reminded him of how important it is to work with other composers.

In an interview with TechRadar Gaming, where the Mass Effect 1 and 2 composer also reacted to BioWare's closure, Wall shared what it was like creating a sci-fi RPG score with Sam Hulick, Richard Jacques, and David Kates.

Industry observers note that "This was the game that helped me understand the value, importance, and just how much fun and rewarding collaborating with other composers can be," Wall remarked. "I’m a decent enough composer, but I feel my real strength is in storytelling and making sure the production and music serve the story and guiding a team to that goal.".

The composer, who also shared how orchestral and synth music influenced the first two games, explained that working with other composers helped the project in the long run, despite his own talents, saying, "It’s sometimes easier to work with other composers to help you fulfill the mandate of having music be this unseen character in the game that really tells the story sonically and helps the player be more immersed in the experience.".

Industry observers note that wall added, "You can suddenly float to the 30,000-foot level and understand how it’s all supposed to work together. Not that you can’t do that on your own, but it’s just easier, more fluid, and you get there in sort of a 1 + 1 = 3 way.

"I like that insta-grat [instant gratification] of having the music finished sooner so you can really play with it and hone it.".

Elsewhere, Wall also shared his stance on artificial intelligence being used as a replacement in video games, saying, "AI is not an artist.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the battery on the Pixel Tag is rated for about a year, but what happens when you need to replace it? Here’s how to replace it.

Due to the shape and design of the Pixel Tag, you might have a bit of difficulty getting the backplate off rapidly to throw in a fresh battery when it’s time.

Having had a few problems myself (yes, a me problem most likely) due to the slick, smooth shape, I figured that, even though it might insult the intelligence of many, the process was at least documented so that anyone having issues has a reference to come to if they’re struggling to get that backplate off.

Sources indicate that you will have difficulty if you try to do this one-handed. Instead, clasp the Pixel Tag with one thumb at the base or midframe, then with your other thumb twist anticlockwise until the backplate comes loose and the battery will drop out.

In a recent development, the first time you do this, it will be harder due to the tight factory seal. However, once it’s open, the process gets easier to replicate. Here’s a little demonstration of how to get it off without it slipping and being flung into the ether:.

It has been revealed that be aware that you may need to open and reseat the battery if Find Hub does not recognize the Pixel Tag again when you’ve done this. Even with the factory-supplied battery, it can misalign if you don’t place it in the correct position and fully close the door when reassembling.

If you’re wondering what type of battery you need, CR2032 are the standard for watches and most Android trackers. They’re super cheap with a 10-pack of Amazon Basics batteries for just $10, Duracell offers a 4-pack for under $7 but you can even get unbranded 20-packs for around $9. All fairly cheap at various points in the quality spectrum.

It can’t hurt to have some on hand when you do eventually need to replace the battery in your Pixel Tag. You can get the tracker from Amazon and the Google Store right now.

  • In a recent development, once a random hardware nerd lawyer on Reddit, the lawyer's responses to the original breaking story illuminated his identity.
  • Sources indicate that he built the software side with AI, specifically Claude Code, which wrote the kernels and ran the benchmarks with his direction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A lawyer with a private AI server built on eight used Nvidia V100 GPUs returned with an enhancement, moving about 80% of its work up from 2-bit to 4-bit NVFP4 precision and bringing in 1TB of RAM and an RTX 3090. The server uses DeepSeek V4.1 Flash with a legal harness, the workflows and checks he wraps around the model, for his law practice. The cost? Performance, with code output dropping from 160–215 to 150–180 tokens per second, although the crashes that hit the latest build are gone. The culprit behind the crashes, originally blamed on PCIe, was likely a bad PSU.

In a recent development, once a random hardware nerd lawyer on Reddit, the lawyer's responses to the original breaking story illuminated his identity. He’s a trial lawyer in Columbia, South Carolina. ProprietaryLegalAI commented on our first story three times, linking to a code repository, site, and LinkedIn that identify him as Nick Mermiges, founder of PLI Labs and proprietarylegal.ai. His other firm, PLI, is a technology consultancy, not a law firm, and now lists private, on-prem LLM serving as a service.

Sources indicate that he built the software side with AI, specifically Claude Code, which wrote the kernels and ran the benchmarks with his direction. The Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 models handled the optimizations, custom kernels, and re-quantizing; he noted he was surprised at how well Fable built custom Volta kernels, and how it re-quantizes the experts his legal harness triggers. From about February to July, he built a legal harness around Claude that worked, while his attempts at a local-model version failed, but then DeepSeek V4.1 Flash arrived, and he was able to port it successfully, even if he says it’s not as good as frontier.

He reaffirms that “the documents never leave the office” and upgraded the system from 256GB to 1TB of RAM and tossed in a newer GPU, even as the V100s stay on “borrowed time” with R580, the last Nvidia driver branch to support them. The project’s intentions, as listed last time, suggested he wanted the system to be able to offload more of his workload, so this and the precision change are a reasonable upgrade. His previously stated goal of wanting the system to handle more than one request at a time has also been met.

The original “Volta sPLIt” build we covered has transformed into the “Volta Max uPLIft,” still with the clever lettering as his manufacturer’s initials are PLI — Proprietary Legal Intelligence. He now claims “near-NVFP4 precision,” having described NVFP4 on our forum earlier this week as “essentially full precision.” NVFP4 is Nvidia’s 4-bit floating-point format, and Nvidia publishes its own NVFP4 version of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; the project’s README says that version matches the precision of the model’s official weights at 4.25 bits per weight.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is built from “experts,” the parts of the model that do most of the work for each word. This model didn’t fit at that precision before, as 384 routed experts, in each of 40 layers, counts to 15,360 in all. At official precision, this comes out to about 269 GiB, by his estimate, and eight 32GB V100s have 256 GiB in total before anything else is loaded. With the 2-bit build, the weights were 248.8GB; the new build’s Hugging Face package is about 556GB.

Recent findings suggest that the workaround is to keep every expert on the cards at 2-bit and swap the most-used ones up until the cards are full, which in this case came out to about 38.7%, or 5,949 experts, at precisely NVFP4. “Most-used,” in this context, refers to a count from a mix of four kinds of text, which are weighted equally, one of which is his own legal harness traffic.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Industry observers note that the payoff is that those experts do most of the work. In testing with one request at a time, between 80% and 86% of decode routes, the calls to an expert made while the model writes, land on the NVFP4 experts, lowest for general text and highest for source code. The prediction for the two-request setup he runs is 78% to 85%. The remaining 15% to 22% of calls would still go to a 2-bit expert.

According to recent reports, measured against Nvidia’s own version of the model as the reference, he was able to get good results. Same next token, or how often a build picks the same next token as the reference, went up to 95.1% from 92.2%. For KL divergence, which measures how far a build’s probabilities are from the reference’s, it went down to 0.079 nats from 0.196. In measuring multiple-choice answers that change, across 513 questions from a standard multiple-choice knowledge test, it went from 79 different to just 8.

This does not measure accuracy — which was about the same across all three cases — but fidelity. Those tests ran on the build’s first release, but not on the latest two-request setup he now runs.

The result of the changes: higher fidelity but at a lower level of performance. Code output is 3% to 30% slower, depending on the prompt length, and legal writing is 9% to 23% slower. Before the build, he hoped to maintain about 80 tokens per second on legal and prose; the bench came in at 86 to 106 for legal and 78 to 86 for prose. The upside is that running two requests at once raises total output to 159.0 tokens per second, versus 118.9 with a sole request. The first token also arrives sooner at every prompt length, 108.4 seconds versus 118.7 seconds at 256K tokens.

Each request needs a “slot,” though, and this comes at a cost. Every slot keeps its own state on the cards, which leaves room for fewer NVFP4 experts: 6,215, 5,949, 5,663 for one, two, and three slots, respectively. This means each added slot may push another one to two points of the calls back to 2-bit, which could reduce output quality.

Recent findings suggest that builder’s measurements, Nov. 5 (2-bit) and Nov. 12 (near-NVFP4); greedy decoding, thinking off, one request at a time.

Industry observers note that the move to more RAM came this week with eight 128GB modules at 2,933 MT/s, originally eight 32GB modules that had to be run at DDR4-2666 due to ECC errors. After the RAM upgrade, the host reports two NUMA nodes, and two boots hung at the first transfer between the boards, so he reordered the cards in software. The GPUs remain capped at 1,522 MHz, as before.

As for the PSU, he took the common approach of chasing PCIe slots, cards, and cables to narrow down the cause, finally concluding it was “probably one bad PSU.” He also added more fans, but with no temperature changes, this only indicated that airflow was not the problem. He changed the power delivery, and nine of nine long chats read clean afterward. Also, don’t judge his cable management skill; any “advice [there] is welcome and will be ignored,” which is the only comment to make in that situation.

He also already has two DGX Sparks running the same model at 1M context for agent work, and three or four sessions at once, and he isn’t stopping there. Now it comes down to scaling. Eight more V100s and a second server, with 512GB of 3,200 MT/s ECC RAM, are waiting in the wings. The second box would run another high-precision DeepSeek, used as an extra agent or to run tasks in parallel. The plan is also to move DeepSeek’s small draft model off the V100s and onto the RTX 3090, which hasn’t happened yet.

Presentation: The Influence Toolkit
